💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that how do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world?
  • While the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media.
  • It has been revealed that the data also indicates that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that how do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, indicates that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly important tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.

While the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report says.

It has been revealed that the data also indicates that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report states. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”.

According to recent reports, when it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents said they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).

A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.

Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also revealed that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.

Recent findings suggest that the importance of ​​online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among new collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.

But can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.

In a recent development, the report interestingly states that the youngest generation of collectors—Gen Z—are not the ones using social media the most in their collecting journeys. “The generation raised on social media is, it turns out, the one most inclined to keep its collecting close,” the report notes. While the data highlighted that Gen Z were the highest-spending generation surveyed and had the most wide-ranging collecting habits, their awareness of digital footprints leads them to seek greater control and privacy over their "personal and cultural identities".

“Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”.

When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

I Couldn’t Imagine Working With a Photo Editor on a Different Continent

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Long before I worked on the PetaPixel news desk, I was an agency photographer covering breaking news, features, and sports.
  • I was young and in need of guidance.
  • I would speak to Gary every morning when he assigned me jobs for the day, talking me through what was expected and the specific set of photos I needed to produce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long before I worked on the PetaPixel news desk, I was an agency photographer covering breaking news, features, and sports.

I was young and in need of guidance. I found that in the form of my photo editor, whom I’m going to call Gary.

I would speak to Gary every morning when he assigned me jobs for the day, talking me through what was expected and the specific set of photos I needed to produce.

After I wired him the photos, he would let me know whether I had done a good job or a terrible one.

He would often edit my photos, reframe them slightly, change the crop, cull some of them, or call me up and ask if I had a different angle.

But Gary did far more than that. He was a leader in the newsroom, worked closely with the news editor to shape stories and come up with ideas, and was an excellent salesman.

Sources indicate that his vivacious personality helped. He invented nicknames for me and the other photographers, made silly jokes, and was just generally good for staff morale. Not everyone liked the owners, but everyone liked Gary.

Industry observers note that after I had worked there for a few years, the agency was bought out, and Gary moved to a new hub hundreds of miles away. Our relationship was never the same. The new regime was different, and I left soon after.

I thought of Gary this week when the Associated Press officially cut all eight of the remaining photo editor positions in the U.S.

Industry observers note that AP has moved the positions to its hub in Noida, India. The agency claims it has looks to grow the Indian operation to 100 staff members, including video producers.

AP photo editors are legendary: Consider the famous Napalm Girl photograph, for example, when Horst Faas and Hal Buell overruled Carl Robinson’s decision not to wire Nick Ut’s photograph.

Photo editors have played a crucial role in the fortunes of photographers for a very long time, advocating for us while seeing the bigger picture.

It’s not a question of whether talented photo editors exist in India. Of course, they do. But there’s something valuable about having an editor who understands the local news environment, knows the photographers personally, and can build relationships over years of working together.

Recent findings suggest that and look, I get it: the press industry is tough. Agency bosses were once raking in vast sums of money — these days they face lousy picture rates from a fractured industry.

It has been revealed that photo editors do not attend a news story in person the way photographers do; therefore, they could theoretically be anywhere. This is a globalized, technologized world: workers in developing countries are technically in competition with workers from the U.S.

But while these massive decisions make sense from a financial point of view, what are the long-term consequences?

Photographers, like my younger self, have fewer opportunities to benefit from a leading light like Gary.

Nowadays, photographers are increasingly expected to be fully formed; the bosses need someone they can rely on to do a good job no matter what. And while there are plenty of great photographers out there who can do that, they all had to cut their teeth somewhere.

As with many other things in life, it feels like the ladder for the younger generation is being removed.

Hilma af Klint's painting “Ser III No. 5” (1920) sold for a record $12.7 million (SEK 128.9 million) at Bukowskis's modern art and design auction in Stockholm today, November 19, fetching over 16 times the upper end of its estimated price.

The first abstract painting by the Swedish artist and "mother of abstraction" to appear on the open market in 30 years, "Ser III No. 5" was one of the 85 geometric paintings the artist produced during a fervent months-long process in 1920. Theosophical symbols, triangles, and circles in "Ser III No. 5" provide insight into af Klint's last engagement with geometric abstraction before she turned to more naturalist watercolors in the last years of her life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Black and White Photo Awards 2026 winners have been unveiled. Photographers competed across six categories, each vying to be named Black and White Photographer of the Year.

Speaking of which, this year’s significant winner is Shengwei Dai, who took the top spot for a spectacular shot of a man jumping between two moving trains, with dozens of passengers looking on.

Dai earned a €1,500 cash prize for the win, the largest single award in the competition’s five-year history.

Alongside Dai’s overall win, competition judges selected winners across six categories: Architecture, Fauna and Flora, Landscape, Portrait, Street, and the new Open Theme.

“The new category aims to welcome photographs that, through their artistic, narrative, or conceptual approach, do not fit neatly into any of the traditional disciplines,” the Black and White Photo Awards explains.

Each category also includes Golden, Silver, and Bronze mentions, which serve as runner-up and honorable mention distinctions. Category winners each receive a €200 cash prize.

Photographer Qian Shen won the Architecture category with a striking shot of the Suzhou Olympic Sports Center in China.

Mohammad Mirza’s photo, Silent Majesty, earned the top spot in the Fauna and Flora category. The image captures a white rhinoceros emerging through the mist and trees in Kenya’s Solio Reserve, a private wildlife sanctuary.

Jie Fischer’s Flamingo in Flight 2 bested the competition in the Landscape category. The nearly abstract aerial shot captures a flock of flying flamingos from a top-down perspective against a high-contrast, pattern-filled terrain.

Happy Mukherjee’s portrait, Behind the Silence, depicts a young girl and invites viewers to wonder about her expression and gaze.

Sources indicate that cow Watching by Chongfeng Wu won the Street category. Unlike most street photos captured in urban environments, Wu’s pastoral shot is much quieter.

The inaugural Open Theme winner is Lloyd Lane, whose image, Convergence, captures a flock of starlings over Brighton Palace Pier in England.

The judges also selected finalists across all six categories, and their work can be viewed on the Black and White Photo Awards website.

The Black and White Photo Awards is already looking forward to its sixth annual competition in 2027, with entries opening on January 1.

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

It has been revealed that the Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College announced Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in Latest York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.

So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.

According to recent reports, “The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”.

Between Moonlight and Aurora: Photographing East Greenland After Dark

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that photographing East Greenland at night is an exercise in preparation, observation, and adaptation.
  • During a recent photography expedition in East Greenland, hosted by Secret Atlas this last October 2026, I spent several evenings leading the photographic project targeting enormous icebergs illuminated by the rising moon, alongside the Northern Lights appearing above the surrounding fjords and ice.
  • In a recent development, some photographs begin long before the camera is taken out of the bag.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that photographing East Greenland at night is an exercise in preparation, observation, and adaptation. The landscape is immense, the conditions can be demanding, and the opportunities to make a particular image may be limited to a few minutes. Towering icebergs, drifting sea ice, fog, low clouds, and the changing Arctic sky create an environment in which light can completely transform the way a scene is perceived. Yet having spectacular scenery in front of you does not necessarily mean you will come away with a strong photograph. The challenge is to recognize what makes a moment worth capturing, understand how the available light interacts with the landscape, and make the right decisions before that moment disappears.

During a recent photography expedition in East Greenland, hosted by Secret Atlas this last October 2026, I spent several evenings leading the photographic project targeting enormous icebergs illuminated by the rising moon, alongside the Northern Lights appearing above the surrounding fjords and ice. These two subjects offered very different photographic challenges and a particular one-of-a-kind night operation.

In a recent development, some photographs begin long before the camera is taken out of the bag. The moonrise series was one of those projects. Across four days, I followed the changing opportunities to photograph the rising moon among the enormous icebergs of East Greenland. The objective was not simply to record the moon above the horizon, but to find a relationship between the moonlight, the architecture of the icebergs, the sense of exploration, and the surrounding landscape.

In a recent development, the first opportunity to photograph the sequence came around 8 p.m. on day three of our expedition, when the timing and the available light finally began to align. In the Arctic, twilight can retain considerable ambient light even as the moon rises. This transition creates an interesting balance: the landscape may still hold detail, while the moon begins illuminating the ice from a different angle.

A rising moon and a monumental iceberg are impressive subjects individually, but putting them together is not enough. Their positions, relative sizes, illumination, and separation from the background all influence how the image is read. Anticipating these relationships is essential, particularly when the window for making the photograph is short.

According to recent reports, photographing from a Zodiac adds another dimension to the process. Polar bear presence in East Greenland limits our possibility to operate on land during low-light conditions. Unlike working from stable ground, the shooting position is not necessarily fixed, and even small movements can affect the framing, particularly when using a long focal length.

The objective was to find a viewpoint from which the iceberg formations could be separated visually and the rising moon incorporated without losing the sense of scale. Icebergs are difficult subjects to photograph because their dimensions can be hard to communicate.

Focal length plays an important role in communicating scale. A wide-angle lens can emphasize the surrounding environment, while a longer lens can compress the scene and bring distant formations visually closer together.

Sources indicate that exposure requires similar care. A gradually brightening moon against a dark sky can make it difficult to preserve highlights without losing detail in the shadows. Rather than trying to make every part of the photograph equally bright, I aim to retain the texture of the illuminated surfaces while allowing darkness to remain part of the image, preserving my highlight and shadow information.

According to recent reports, the Northern Lights create a very different set of challenges. The moon’s position can be anticipated, allowing me to plan around a relatively predictable source of illumination. This is great for subject illumination, though distracting when the moon appears in the frame. The aurora, by contrast, can change rapidly in brightness, shape, color, and movement.

Sources indicate that from our main vessel, we navigate through the fjord in search of a good-looking iceberg to frame our shot. We carefully position the ship to achieve the greatest possible stability while maintaining the flexibility to adjust our orientation depending on where the aurora is expected to appear. The moment the Northern Lights emerge, close coordination via VHF radio with the bridge team becomes essential. As we prepare to photograph from the ship’s outer deck, the vessel is brought to a complete standstill, reaching zero speed over ground. This allows us to capture the scene with maximum stability, even using exposures of around half a second, while the iceberg and the dancing aurora create the perfect natural composition.

Aurora photography involves a series of compromises between shutter speed, aperture, and ISO. A longer exposure collects more light, which can help when the display is faint, but it can also blur the finer structures of a rapidly moving aurora. A shorter exposure preserves more detail in the curtains and patterns but requires enough light to produce a usable image. There is no universal exposure for the Northern Lights. The right settings depend on the brightness and speed of the display, the available ambient light, the lens, and the amount of detail I want to retain. I adjust according to the behavior of the sky rather than relying on a fixed recipe, as shown below with this powerful curtain of light.

As the sun began to set, we left the comfort of our main vessel and ventured out aboard our Zodiacs for a reconnaissance ride through the surrounding waters. Our mission was to explore the landscape, identify one or two particularly striking icebergs, and select the perfect setting for what we hoped would become an unforgettable night of aurora photography. Capturing the Northern Lights is as much about patience and preparation as it is about being in the right place at the right time. With exposures ranging from half a second to four, five, or even six seconds, stability becomes essential. Even the slightest movement can compromise an image. Out here, surrounded by the vastness of the polar landscape, finding a way to create a stable photographic platform would be one of the greatest challenges of the night.

According to recent reports, our idea was to return after dark, launching the Zodiacs from the main vessel and navigating through the freezing waters in search of newly formed sea ice near one of the selected icebergs. This young ice, approximately one centimeter thick, offered the possibility of carefully positioning the bow of a Zodiac against its edge, allowing us to wedge ourselves into place and create the stability required for long exposures. Finding a sufficiently wide area of newly formed ice would also give us the freedom to reposition ourselves as the auroras shifted and danced across different parts of the sky. But this was about more than simply finding a stable platform. It was about finding the right perspective, in pitch darkness surrounded by the freezing Greenlandic waters.

It has been revealed that when planning an operation like this, I always look for ways to approach an iceberg while maintaining a safe distance and shooting from as low an angle as possible. I want the iceberg to become a powerful element in the composition, rising beneath the aurora and giving the image a strong sense of scale and depth. The newly formed sea ice often adds another dimension to the scene. Its delicate patterns, textures, and natural leading lines can guide the viewer’s eye toward the main subject, transforming an already extraordinary landscape into a compelling photographic composition.

It has been revealed that by 11 p.m., it was time. We left the main vessel and began our night mission. Alongside my teammates Signe-Maria and Myriam, I led our group of photographers toward the giant icebergs and the newly formed sea ice. Behind us, the ship’s powerful searchlight illuminated our chosen iceberg, providing a guiding beacon across the darkness as we made our way toward our destination. Once we reached the area, we carefully positioned the Zodiacs against the edge of the newly formed ice. Every movement had to be deliberate. We wanted to achieve the stability needed for photography while maintaining a safe distance from the iceberg and the surrounding ice.

According to recent reports, fortunately, we had prepared for this moment long before leaving the ship. During the day, we had already assembled, adjusted, and practiced our photographic setups, making sure everyone knew exactly what to do. Now, under the darkness of the polar night, there was no time to waste. We secured our tripods against the Zodiac’s pontoon and tilted them forward, carefully adjusting their position to keep every part of the Zodiac out of the frame. One by one, our photographers settled into their compositions, pointing their cameras toward the magnificent icebergs.

Everything was ready. I picked up the radio and called the ship’s bridge team, asking them to switch off all the lights. And suddenly, everything changed. The powerful beam that had guided us across the darkness disappeared. We were now completely immersed in the polar night, resting on the newly formed sea ice, facing a gigantic iceberg beneath an extraordinary celestial spectacle. Above us, twenty billion stars seemed to fill the sky. A half-moon gently illuminated the frozen landscape, revealing the magnificent shapes and textures of the iceberg, while the auroras began dancing overhead, bringing movement and color to an otherwise silent world.

For a moment, everything seemed to stand still. There we were, floating between the ocean and the ice, surrounded by one of the most extraordinary landscapes on Earth. Cameras were clicking, shutters were opening and closing, and each long exposure was capturing a fleeting moment of this ever-changing spectacle. It is difficult to describe the feeling of witnessing such a scene. You can initiative every detail, prepare your equipment, study the conditions, and carefully orchestrate the entire operation, but nature always has the final word. And when everything finally comes together, the experience goes far beyond photography. That night, we were fortunate enough to experience something truly exceptional. A moment in which preparation, teamwork, adventure, and nature converged beneath the dancing auroras. The photographs will remain on our SD cards, but the feeling of being there, surrounded by the icebergs, the stars, and the silence of the polar night, will remain with us forever.

There is a tendency to describe photographs of the Arctic as the result of being in the right place at the right time. Luck certainly plays a role. The moon must rise in a favorable position, the weather must allow the landscape to be seen, and the aurora must develop in a way that creates an interesting composition. None of these conditions can be guaranteed. But being present when a spectacle occurs is only part of the process. The photographer must recognize the potential of the scene, decide where to position the camera, choose a focal length, balance the exposure, and determine which elements belong in the frame. Preparation does not control nature; it makes it possible to respond when an opportunity appears.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, nothing in visual culture is neutral, least of all the color wheel itself. Scholar Richard Powell explores this deceptively simple truth in his upcoming book, tackling the theoretical entanglement of race and pigment and how Black painters have used color over time. Trailblazing art historian Lowery Stokes Sims, formerly a curator at the Met Museum and director of the Studio Museum in Harlem, parses his richly layered essays today, linking the critical theory of Josef Albers and Darby English to the practices of artists like Jacob Lawrence and Alma Thomas. The book, Sims writes, shifted the way she’ll look at art moving forward.

Meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum: News broke that a 1920 painting by Hilma af Klint sold for $12.7 million. Yes, the same Hilma af Klint who described herself less as an artist and more as a channel for a higher power, who followed the guidance of spirits that took physical form through her paintings. But hey, at least the painting’s owner has a new addition to their investment portfolio?

According to recent reports, in reviews, Alina Cohen spends time with the poignant, impactful photographs by Laia Abril, who evokes the systems of patriarchy and sexual violence through the quietly haunting garments and objects in their wake. As the Cornell 7 case continues and convicted abusers sit in office, Abril’s photographs “reject both the invisibility of some crimes and the all-too-visible nature of others.” More, as always, below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books.

According to recent reports, I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of important theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026). | Lowery Stokes Sims.

Just Released: Monoprints by Tala Madani.

Iconic and Independent: Latest York Studio School’s MFA Program.

According to recent reports, in her latest show, garments and other objects serve as stand-ins for the systems that allow sexual assault to persist. | Alina Cohen.

In a recent development, her candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy. | Eileen G’Sell.

Contemporary Beadworker Ken Williams Jr Awarded Rakow Commission by Corning Museum of Glass.

Latest Update: Layered Compositions Will Level Up Your Landscape Photography

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A landscape can look dramatically different in person than it does in a photograph, particularly when a scene loses its sense of depth and scale.
  • Recent findings suggest that creating depth in landscape photography starts with understanding how different parts of a scene relate to one another.
  • Recent findings suggest that getting those elements to work together takes more than placing an interesting subject in the foreground or pointing the camera at a dramatic mountain range.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A landscape can look dramatically different in person than it does in a photograph, particularly when a scene loses its sense of depth and scale. Explore how thoughtful layering brings distant views to life by connecting nearby details with the features that make a location memorable.

Recent findings suggest that creating depth in landscape photography starts with understanding how different parts of a scene relate to one another. Foreground details establish scale, middle-ground features connect the viewer to the wider landscape, and distant elements provide context. When these elements complement one another, they give the photograph greater dimension and draw the viewer through the frame.

Recent findings suggest that getting those elements to work together takes more than placing an interesting subject in the foreground or pointing the camera at a dramatic mountain range. Camera position, focal length, overlapping shapes, and changing light all influence how layers appear and how easily the viewer can distinguish them. This guide explores how to apply these techniques in the field—from recognizing natural layers and arranging them within the frame to avoiding visual clutter.

It has been revealed that the foundation of a layered landscape composition is the relationship between its foreground, middle ground, and background. These three zones provide a visual structure that communicates distance and gives the viewer a sense of moving through the scene. The foreground is the area closest to the camera, the middle ground occupies the space between the viewer and the distant scenery, and the background typically contains the farthest elements, such as mountains, hills, or the sky.

Each layer serves a distinct purpose. The foreground anchors the immediate setting and gives the viewer an entry point. The middle ground bridges that starting point to the rest of the landscape, while the background provides context, scale, and a sense of distance. When these elements work together, the photograph feels far more dimensional than a composition built around a single distant subject.

Recent findings suggest that not every landscape needs three clearly defined layers. A photograph of a mountain reflected in a lake, for example, might rely on two dominant planes, while a forest scene could contain several overlapping layers of trees. The goal is not to force every scene into a rigid formula, but to recognize the distinct planes of distance within it and decide how each contributes to the composition.

Before setting up the camera, take a moment to identify what occupies each part of the view. Look for elements that naturally lead the eye through the frame, as well as areas that might compete for attention. Taking this step helps determine whether the scene already has a strong visual structure or whether changing your position could reveal a more effective arrangement.

A strong foreground gives a landscape photograph an immediate point of entry. Rocks, grasses, wildflowers, fallen trees, shoreline details, and other nearby features establish a sense of place while making the distance feel more pronounced. Rather than simply filling the bottom of the frame, the foreground should serve a clear purpose in the composition.

According to recent reports, look for foreground elements that relate to the larger scene. A line of rocks leading toward a mountain, a patch of wildflowers beneath a distant ridgeline, or a weathered tree framing a valley can connect the viewer to the landscape beyond. These details establish scale and make an expansive scene feel more tangible.

It has been revealed that camera position has a considerable effect on how prominent the foreground becomes. Lowering the camera gives nearby objects greater visual weight, often exaggerating their apparent size relative to the background. This can create a dramatic sense of depth, particularly when using a wide-angle lens. However, getting too close can make a foreground object overwhelm the rest of the photograph. Move the camera forward and backward while checking how much space the foreground occupies and whether it remains connected to the distant view.

Pay attention to the edges of the frame as well. A partially cropped rock, branch, or other object along the border can look accidental if it draws attention without adding to the composition. Sometimes shifting the camera just a few inches is enough to position the foreground more deliberately. If there is no suitable foreground element, resist the urge to include something merely to fill the space. A clean, uncomplicated foreground is often more effective than one that distracts from the landscape.

Industry observers note that the middle ground is often the most overlooked part of a landscape composition. Photographers frequently concentrate on finding an interesting foreground and capturing a dramatic background, leaving the space between them without a clear visual role. Yet this middle zone is essential because it bridges near and distant elements, helping the photograph feel cohesive.

Industry observers note that middle-ground subjects can include rolling hills, tree lines, rivers, fields, valleys, waterfalls, or clusters of rocks. These features smooth the transition between planes of distance and can create a natural path through the image. A river winding between a foreground shoreline and distant mountains, for example, gives the viewer a route through the landscape. A series of hills can create successive bands that gradually recede toward the horizon.

It has been revealed that look for shapes and lines that link different parts of the scene. A sloping hillside might echo the angle of a nearby rock formation, while a line of trees could guide attention toward a distant peak. Repeating forms also help unify a composition; a series of ridges or tree-covered slopes creates a visual rhythm that reinforces depth.

If the middle ground feels empty, consider whether changing your position reveals more of the landscape between the foreground and background. Moving laterally along a trail or shoreline can shift the relationship between overlapping features and expose details that were previously hidden. You may also find that a slightly longer focal length brings distant layers together more effectively, especially in landscapes with repeating hills or ridgelines.

The background gives a landscape its broader context, but distant elements can easily lose definition when they blend together. A mountain peak that merges with a similarly toned ridge, for example, may lose its shape and visual impact. Creating separation between background features preserves their individual forms and reinforces the sense of distance.

In a recent development, light and weather often provide natural separation. Sidelighting reveals the contours of distant mountains, while low-angle sunlight casts alternating bands of brightness and shadow across hillsides. Fog, mist, and atmospheric haze also distinguish successive layers by reducing contrast as the landscape recedes. These conditions produce subtle tonal transitions that make distant features appear farther away.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

Camera position matters, too. A slight change in elevation or angle can separate a mountain from the ridge behind it or reveal a gap between two overlapping peaks. Before taking the photograph, examine the outlines of distant features and look for places where they merge. Moving even a short distance can create enough separation to make the shapes easier to read.

Sources indicate that exposure also affects how well those details are retained. Bright skies behind dark mountains often create a wide dynamic range, particularly at sunrise and sunset. Check the histogram and highlight warnings to avoid losing important sky detail. If necessary, use exposure bracketing or a graduated neutral density filter to manage the difference in brightness. Preserving tonal detail across the scene helps maintain the distinction between distant layers.

Recent findings suggest that overlap is one of the most direct ways to communicate depth in a landscape photograph. When one object partially obscures another, the viewer immediately recognizes that the two elements occupy different planes of distance. A foreground tree overlapping a distant ridge, for example, creates a clear spatial relationship even though the photograph is a two-dimensional image.

In a recent development, look for natural arrangements where landscape features overlap cleanly. Successive mountain ridges, layers of trees, and rolling hills are particularly useful because they provide repeated shapes at different distances. The viewer can follow these forms as they recede into the background, creating a sense of depth without requiring a prominent foreground subject.

How much elements overlap also matters. If one element completely hides another, the relationship between them becomes less obvious. If the objects barely touch, their outlines can merge into an awkward visual intersection. Small changes in camera position can reveal more of one feature or create a cleaner separation between them.

This is especially key when photographing forests or densely layered landscapes. Branches and tree trunks can easily intersect in ways that make the image feel tangled. Rather than trying to include every interesting tree, look for openings where individual trunks and branches remain distinguishable. A slight shift to the left or right may separate one tree from another and make the overall arrangement easier to read.

According to recent reports, focal length directly influences how distance and scale appear in the finished photograph. Wide-angle lenses are useful when the foreground is an important part of the composition. Their broad field of view captures nearby details alongside distant scenery, while perspective exaggeration between close and far objects emphasizes depth.

When using a wide-angle lens, foreground placement becomes particularly vital. An object close to the camera can appear much larger than everything behind it, sometimes dominating the frame. This can be effective when the foreground has a strong shape or texture, but it can also make the composition feel unbalanced. Pay attention to how close you are to the nearest subject and whether its scale supports the relationship between layers.

Telephoto lenses offer a different approach. Rather than emphasizing the distance between foreground and background, longer focal lengths narrow the field of view and make distant features appear closer together. This visual compression can emphasize repeated layers of mountains, hills, trees, or other landscape elements. A scene that looks relatively open through a wide-angle lens may reveal a more graphic arrangement when photographed with a telephoto lens.

Neither approach is inherently better. A wide-angle lens communicates the scale of an expansive landscape, while a telephoto lens isolates a series of distant forms and emphasizes their relationship. If a scene has several interesting layers, try photographing it at different focal lengths before deciding which version best captures the scene.

Light makes layered landscapes more distinctive by revealing shapes, textures, and tonal differences across planes of distance. The same scene may look relatively flat under even midday light but become far more dimensional when low-angle sunlight creates alternating bands of illumination and shadow.

Sidelighting is particularly useful for emphasizing the contours of hills, mountains, and other landforms. As the sun sits low on the horizon, ridges catch the light while valleys remain in shadow. This creates visual separation between successive layers and gives the scene a stronger sense of form. Backlighting can also be effective, especially when photographing trees, grasses, or other translucent elements in the foreground.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

Recent findings suggest that atmospheric conditions provide another way to distinguish distance. Mist and fog soften the contrast of distant hills and mountains, creating a series of progressively lighter layers. After a storm, breaks in clearing clouds often spotlight individual sections of a landscape while leaving others in shadow. These changing conditions produce natural divisions between foreground, middle ground, and background without requiring strong compositional elements in every part of the frame.

When photographing in changing weather, be prepared to work quickly. Use a tripod when shutter speeds are slow, but avoid relying on one fixed composition if the light is moving across the scene. Take multiple exposures as conditions evolve, particularly when sunlight briefly strikes a distant ridge or a break in the clouds reveals a fresh layer. These short-lived lighting conditions can make a substantial difference to the finished image.

Adding layers can create depth, but it can also introduce too much visual information. A foreground full of rocks, a middle ground crowded with trees, and a background filled with overlapping mountain peaks may leave the viewer unsure where to look. The challenge is deciding which elements contribute to the photograph and which ones make it harder to read.

Start by identifying the primary subject or visual feature. This does not have to be a single object — it might be a mountain range, a winding river, or a series of repeating ridgelines. Once you know what should attract attention, consider whether the other layers support it. A foreground element that pulls the eye away from the main subject may need to be repositioned or excluded from the frame.

Simplifying a composition does not always mean removing entire layers—it often means adjusting how much visual weight each one carries. A smaller foreground can establish context without competing with the background, while an open middle ground gives the viewer’s eye room to travel through the scene. Switching to a longer focal length can also help trim distracting edges or unrelated elements.

Sources indicate that watch for bright highlights, stray branches, and high-contrast objects that pull attention away from the subject. These distractions become more disruptive in a layered composition, where the viewer’s eye is already navigating multiple planes. Scan the entire frame before pressing the shutter—paying close attention to the corners and edges—for anything that interrupts the visual flow. Often, shifting the camera slightly or tightening the crop is enough to clean up the frame.

It has been revealed that even a minor shift in camera position can alter the relationship between every layer in a landscape. Moving forward or backward changes the scale and placement of foreground objects, while stepping laterally can reveal or conceal distant features. Camera height also dictates how much of the ground plane is visible and how smoothly the foreground transitions into the background.

Industry observers note that rather than immediately setting up a tripod at the first scenic overlook, take time to explore the area. Walk along a ridge, follow a shoreline, or look for a slightly elevated vantage point that opens up the landscape. Observe how foreground elements align with distant peaks, trees, or ridges. Often, the strongest composition sits just a few steps away from the obvious viewpoint.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

Once you find a promising spot, a tripod helps you fine-tune height and framing deliberately. Lowering the tripod emphasizes nearby textures, while raising it reveals more of the middle ground. If your tripod has an adjustable center column, extend it sparingly as raising the column too high reduces stability, especially in windy conditions.

Industry observers note that perspective control is also worth considering in scenes with strong vertical lines. Tilting the camera upward causes trees, cliffs, or buildings to converge toward the top of the frame. While that converging effect can work creatively, keeping vertical lines straight requires leveling the camera and adjusting your composition by stepping back or switching to a wider lens. What matters most is whether the perspective reinforces how you want the layers to relate.

Building a layered landscape composition becomes much easier when you approach a scene methodically. Start by identifying the anchor of the view—whether that is a distant peak, a line of trees, a winding river, or light sweeping across a valley. From there, work backward toward the camera to see which nearby elements can serve as an entry point without overpowering the main subject.

Once you have identified potential layers, move around to test different arrangements. Look for foreground features that lead naturally into the middle ground, and check how distant shapes overlap. Watch the gaps between objects so unrelated elements do not merge into awkward outlines. If the scene feels overly busy, simplify with a tighter framing or a longer focal length rather than trying to include everything.

Recent findings suggest that your camera settings should support both the field conditions and the intended depth of the photograph. For a static landscape requiring front-to-back sharpness, a mid-range aperture such as f/8 or f/11 is a reliable starting point. Focus roughly one-third of the way into the scene, then zoom in on your review screen to verify that both the nearest and farthest key elements are sharp. Optimal focus distance depends on focal length, aperture, and proximity to the foreground; if a very close foreground and distant background cannot both be rendered sharply in a single frame, focus stacking is a reliable alternative when the scene is still.

It has been revealed that keep your ISO low when practical, but do not let the pursuit of a noise-free file force an overly slow shutter speed. Wind moving through grasses or foliage often calls for a faster exposure, even if that requires raising your ISO. A tripod eliminates camera shake, but it cannot freeze motion within the landscape itself.

According to recent reports, before leaving a location, photograph the scene using several different focal lengths and compositions. Start with a wider frame that emphasizes the foreground, then try a tighter composition that compresses repeating layers or gives greater weight to the background. I also like revisiting locations under different light and weather, as shifts in atmosphere or time of day can completely transform a scene’s character and yield a more dramatic photograph. Comparing these variations helps reveal which arrangement and conditions best capture the landscape.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, layered landscape photography is about building intentional relationships between elements in a scene. Foreground, middle ground, and background offer a reliable structural framework, but their impact depends on how well they connect, overlap, and remain visually distinct. By paying close attention to camera position, focal length, light, and visual balance, you can create landscapes with genuine depth and clarity.

Industry observers note that welcome to the 364th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Rei Xiao paints a world of surreal, feline figuration into being while navigating the artist visa system and managing their studio assistant (a dignified cat named Astrid).

Industry observers note that want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.

How long have you been working in this space?

Describe an average day in your studio.

I work from my apartment. The most predictable parts of my studio day start with putting on my sunscreen and painting clothes. It’s a very small space that I paint in, so I usually have to push stuff aside when I start, like my painting cart, stool, and trash bin. I, then, turn on my air purifier, open the lids of my palettes, scrape paints from the previous session, and play either TV reveals I’m familiar with or podcasts hosted by comedians in the background. The day usually ends with my cleaning the palette, emptying and wiping my brush cleaning tank, and diligently washing my brushes. Then I wash my face and go to sleep.

Construction underway on Jean Nouvel's landmark opera house in China

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Located on the Shekou Peninsula overlooking Shenzhen Bay, the opera house will eventually be defined by an elongated, wavy roofscape, nodding to the site’s connection to the sea.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

French architecture studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel has shared photos revealing construction progress on the giant Shenzhen Opera House, due for completion in China in 2028.

Located on the Shekou Peninsula overlooking Shenzhen Bay, the opera house will eventually be defined by an elongated, wavy roofscape, nodding to the site’s connection to the sea.

Pritzker Prize-winning architect Jean Nouvel’s studio has designed it as a latest cultural landmark for the city, with a 2,300-seat concert hall, an 1,800-seat theatre and an 800-seat venue among its facilities.

The construction photos help visualise the scale of the 250,000-square-metre opera house, with its various facilities sprawling out across its waterfront site.

They showcase its main concert hall with its horseshoe-shaped plan, alongside the two smaller performance venues.

Ateliers Jean Nouvel’s design for Shenzhen Opera House was the winning entry of an invited international architecture competition, for which other entrants included SUBSTANTIAL, Snøhetta, MVRDV and Kengo Kuma.

Alongside the main performance halls, it will contain a multifunctional theatre with 400 seats, cultural spaces, backstage areas, apartments for performers and offices.

To help further connect the building to the surrounding water, the interior is expected to feature iridescent materials such as mother-of-pearl, also known as nacre.

“The sea will be both around you and over you,” explained Nouvel when the project was revealed in 2021.

“This explains more clearly why the main foyer has to be made of a noble, precious and luminous material that spells the meeting of sea and music and light,” Nouvel continued.

“Using the lustrous white reflections of a nacreous material will be a concrete poeticisation of the meeting of the sea and the auditorium and concert halls of the Opera House.”.

French architect Nouvel founded his eponymous studio in 1994. We recently reported on the news that the studio’s La Querola housing development in Andorra, designed with Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos, was damaged in a fire. The project won the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards, which took place last night.

Another landmark opera house recently featured on Dezeen is the Shanghai Grand Opera House, designed by Snøhetta with a giant spiral staircase.

Images courtesy of Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that after 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.

Sources indicate that as fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach.

“It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” mentioned Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic.

According to recent reports, “It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!”.

Industry observers note that while not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center, which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing Arts, the PAMM-inspired building sits right on the water's edge just as the museum does in real life.

“We were as delighted as anyone else to find PAMM in what feels like the biggest video game of all time,” said Alexa Ferra, PAMM's senior director of marketing and communications, in an email to Hyperallergic.

Ferra attached a photo someone sent her from the game showing the PAMM dupe and some gummy bear-inspired sculptures installed in the shallow water.

“It's a testament to our stunning Herzog & de Meuron building, and goes to show if you stick around long enough, you'll pop up in the unlikeliest — but inevitable — of places.” Ferra added.

It has been revealed that other references to Miami's arts and culture scene include Leonida's Stockyard neighborhood, which directly channels the street murals and warehouse-lined roads of the Wynwood Arts District. It was reported earlier this summer that Rockstar Games had hired over 50 real street artists to design the in-game murals across Stockyard. Owners shared they've spotted the works of street artist Ahol Sniffs Glue (David Anasagasti), among others.

It has been revealed that miami-raised contemporary photographer Josh Aronson also took notice of GTA 6's inclusion of his installation at the Catalina Hotel & Beach Club in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2024, which Rockstar Games incorporated in Vice City's own Catalina Hotel. From Aronson's Florida Boys (2020–) photo series, the photo “Spring” (2024) was made into an enormous sublimated fabric print that hung from the second-story window of the hotel.

The same printed photo, which features a group of cheerful young men photographed from above while floating in water, is shown at Vice City's Catalina Hotel.

According to recent reports, “Florida Boys is my own imagined version of Florida, so I love that it gets to live on in another imagined Florida,” Aronson told Hyperallergic. “The installation at the Catalina was temporary, but in Vice City, someone might stumble upon it years from now. It’s a reminder of the wild ways we encounter art today, and how a work can find fresh life long after it comes down.”.

GTA6's pre-holiday release comes just before Miami Art Week begins early next month. Those dropping in can find some of Aronson's installations on view beyond Vice City at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens and the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami, and also pay homage to the cultural venues and districts that inspired Leonida.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Johnson Banks rebuilds RIBA for its 200th birthday: the RIBA brand identity turns negative space into a bold typographic mark.

Recent findings suggest that the first thing you see is the space between the letters. RIBA arrives as four solid capitals on a pale wall, each letter built from the gaps around it, the R split into a bowl and a leg, the B into two stacked bowls, the A into a triangle over a flat base. It is a mark about architecture made from architecture itself, walls and openings rather than a drawn symbol, and it holds at every size, from a tote bag to a building banner.

The type does the work. Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea. The mark can sit on top of a photograph, cut into it, or anchor a corner or an edge, and the same logic runs through a set of drop capitals, letters drawn to open a page like a doorway.

Industry observers note that the old identity, letters drawn by Eric Gill beside a highly detailed symbol, had drifted over twenty-five years into hundreds of sub-brands with no house style holding them together. The new system pulls them back into line, with related identities for RSAW, the Royal Society of Architects in Wales, and RIBAJ, the institute journal, each sitting inside the same approach, and clear guidelines built on accessible fonts so the brand stays useful and durable.

Colour went back to the beginning. The historic red, the shade the public knows from RIBA signboards, returns front and centre, running across the tote bag, the drawing stencil and the vertical banner on a brick facade. Against it, the palette stays quiet, stone grey, pale blue, black, so the red reads as a signal rather than a decoration, and the crest, the two lions, survives in a simplified, softened form as a quiet sign-off, debossed in black on black.

The system proves itself on the objects architects use. Book spines carry RIBA, RSAW and RIBAJ in red, white and blue on a wooden shelf. A red stencil ruler cuts the letters into a drawing tool. A poster for the Domestic Building Contract pairs a giant yellow D with a red architectural photograph. And the illustration style, flat geometric shapes in red, blue and green with small cut-out figures, gives the brand a way to talk about people without a photograph.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

Recent findings suggest that the act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

Recent findings suggest that for many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

Sources indicate that but here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

According to recent reports, there’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

Sources indicate that one 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

Recent findings suggest that however, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos indicated no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

It has been revealed that in a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings indicated that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

What started as a project to preserve and commemorate these forgotten figures of history soon grew into a broader collaboration across Alabama.

Sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project. The exhibition showcases a series of handmade quilts by Yvonne Wells, Wini McQueen, and Mercedes Braxton, alongside fellow Lowndes County artists including Bill Traylor, Noah Purifoy, and Charlie Lucas, highlighting the region's rich artistic tradition.

According to recent reports, “A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains. “We were really cognizant of our role, to work away from that narrative and work in collaboration with what was already happening at these sites.”.

A transplant herself, Evans hoped to learn about the traditions of Southern artists when she attended the quilt symposium “Every Stitch a Story,” hosted on Auburn’s campus. After Evans heard about the “Sew Their Names” project through a presentation by Judge Susan Walker, she thought it might be a good fit for the Museum in Motion initiative at the Jule. Previously, this initiative supported the 2022 exhibition Spell, Time, Practice, American, Body: The Work of RaMell Ross; Evans herself spearheaded partnerships across Hale County, where Ross’s film Hale County This Morning, This Evening (2018) was made.

Workshops at Auburn University's Rural Studio, November 2024 (both photos Mike Cortez).

It has been revealed that “Since Auburn is a land grant institution, we see that part of our mission is taking the museum beyond our walls and reaching out to other parts of the state,” indicates Christy Barlow, the Museum’s Assistant Director of Education, Engagement, and Learning. Supported by resources from the Jule, “Sew Their Names” traveled around the state, pairing a showcase of quilts by commissioned artists with a series of workshops that allowed community members to participate in the quilt-making process.

The first workshop took place in November 2024, as the exhibition traveled to Hale County, where Auburn’s Rural Studio, an off-campus architecture program focused on rural housing development, is located. The quilts were exhibited at a variety of local venues — what Evans termed a “quilt trail” — including Newbern Library, a project by Rural Studio; Sumac Cottage, an art gallery in Greensboro; and the Safe House Black History Museum, which foregrounded the exhibition’s focus on historical reckoning.

The exhibition then traveled to the Project Threadways Symposium in Florence, Alabama. Founded by designer and textile artist Natalie Chanin, the symposium’s 2025 edition focused on food, clothing, and shelter. The symposium also hosted a quilt-making workshop at the Kennedy-Douglass Center for the Arts in Florence. “Part of the experience of the Mt. Willing quilters is that they also sing as they work,” explains Barlow, who attended many of the in-person workshops. “So the singing is happening, and you have people scattered all throughout this historic house, sewing, learning to sew, learning about this story.”.

By early 2026, the exhibition made its way back to the Jule for a more permanent place in the main gallery; as Barlow explains, this is an unusual trajectory for a curatorial project. “Most of the time, the curatorial side develops an exhibition, and then education responds to it,” she indicates. “However, this was a Museum in Motion initiative which eventually led to an exhibition. When you work that way, you have more input from community voices, who are part of the conversation from the very beginning.”.

Sources indicate that within the exhibition gallery, alongside featured quilts by Wini McQueen, Yvonne Wells, and Mercedes Braxton, other work by fellow Lowndes County natives was showcased. This included a painting by internationally renowned outsider artist Bill Traylor, a vivid three-dimensional collage by Noah Purifoy, a sculpture by Charlie Lucas, and a poster from the Lowndes County Freedom Organization. By pairing works from their permanent collection alongside quilts by the community, the exhibition emphasizes not only the variety of artistic forms across the region, but also the overt political nature of these practices; the Lowndes County Freedom Organization, for example, fought to empower Black voters during a time of extreme violence and intimidation.

It has been revealed that the exhibition soon became a focus of class visits from across Auburn University, drawing students in art history, philosophy, history, and even engineering. “A lot of Alabama-born students may not have a museum in their community,” explains Charlotte Hendrix, the museum’s communications director. “The Jule may be their first encounter walking into a space that can be intimidating; they might feel that they have to know a lot about art. When students participate in the process, you really can’t beat that, in terms of active, engaged learning.”.

SSdH "renegotiates light" in Melbourne warehouse transformation

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A double-height glass atrium draws light into the open-plan interior of Tucker, a former warehouse that Australian architecture practice SSdH has turned into a residence and exhibition space in Melbourne.
  • For the project, SSdH wanted to focus on adaptation over replacement and aimed to work as much as possible with the existing warehouse structure.
  • The studio designed a raised courtyard, a steel-mesh external stair tower and a double-height atrium to draw more natural light into the 770-square-metre space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Pier Carthew.

A double-height glass atrium draws light into the open-plan interior of Tucker, a former warehouse that Australian architecture practice SSdH has turned into a residence and exhibition space in Melbourne.

For the project, SSdH wanted to focus on adaptation over replacement and aimed to work as much as possible with the existing warehouse structure.

The studio designed a raised courtyard, a steel-mesh external stair tower and a double-height atrium to draw more natural light into the 770-square-metre space.

To help retain the character of the former warehouse, SSdH fitted the main entrance into its loading bay and preserved a ghost sign overhead.

The Galvabond-clad entry was designed to act as a “deliberately compressed” holding zone, SSdH said, suspending visitors within a relatively unlit area before opening onto the light-drenched central space.

“Light was a big part of the original brief, with the existing boundary walls, limited openings and previous additions leaving much of the warehouse interior quite dark”, SSdH told Dezeen.

“We liked the idea of being held for a moment, making the shift in scale and light feel more surprising”.

Next to the main entrance, SSdH placed a double-storey external stairway that leads to a roof terrace. This was clad in steel mesh to allow for natural light and views from the first-floor interiors.

The ground floor interior is dominated by a double-height glass and steel atrium that was angled against the original floor plan of the warehouse to let light into the open-plan living area.

“Our approach begins with looking at what’s already there rather than trying to make something entirely fresh”, SSdH mentioned.

“We were interested in how the building could continue to evolve through smaller adjustments rather than extensive demolition”.

The studio designed the interior of the home to be “continuously adaptable”, with the ground floor able to be used as an exhibition space.

Much of the floor initiative is given over to open space, with a curation of select furnishings anchoring it.

In the living area, built-in sofas line the perimeter of the atrium wall next to the courtyard, and are accompanied by an industrial-informed timber and shearling bench by design studio BMDO.

In the kitchen, SSdH added a monolithic travertine island that is complemented by spotted-gum-timber and stainless-steel cabinetry that was fitted against a preserved painted-brick wall.

“Throughout, the material palette is honest, refined and robust, allowing the characters of the original warehouse to remain present”, said SSdH.

A wooden staircase set within a double-height void leads to the first floor, which features wraparound circulation and is home to the private bedrooms and bathrooms.

Spotted-gum and big-river timber cladding was used across cabinetry, extended doorways and flooring, with exposed roof trusses visible throughout. Both bedrooms receive ample light from south and north-facing windows, with the primary bedroom overlooking the atrium and courtyard below.

The main bathroom is fitted with wraparound marble and features a glass brick exterior wall that SSdH added as part of its aim to “renegotiate light” within the existing framework of the warehouse.

“We were drawn to the thickness and form of the glass, which catches, holds and releases light in a way that conventional textured glazing doesn’t quite achieve,” the studio mentioned.

Overall, SSdH hoped to preserve the charm of the original warehouse while creating an adaptable, contemporary space.

Many decisions were “made on site as the building revealed itself”, the studio mentioned.

“We wanted the spaces to remain open to different ways and possibilities of living, allowing the building to adapt without needing to be completely reworked in the future”, it concluded.

Other Melbourne homes recently featured on Dezeen include a studio with a “lantern-like” glass-block facade, a century-old corner shop transformed into a family home and a home comprised of a cluster of red-brick volumes.

Photography by Pier Carthew.
