5 Signs You’re in a One-Sided Friendship, According to Experts

📅 19 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship.
  • Most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going.
  • You might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

Most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going. If that balance consistently feels off—not just once or twice, but over the course of weeks or months—it’s hard not to wonder whether something deeper is going on.

You might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation. They call, if at all, only when they’re bored or when it’s convenient. And then there’s the sharper sting of noticing how effortlessly they find time for other people—just not for you (a surprisingly common frustration you can read more about here).

In a recent development, to be fair, life can get in the way—people get busy, schedules clash, and our friends can’t always be as available as we’d like—but that doesn’t make it any less frustrating or stop you from feeling resentful when you’re waiting days for a simple “How are you?” But how do you know if this is a temporary lapse or a more unhealthy one-sided friendship? Here are the biggest red flags therapists want you to watch out for.

In a recent development, look through your texts and DMs: Are you always the first to send a message? When’s the last time they suggested hanging out? You can also experiment by not reaching out to see how long it takes for them to initiate contact. If weeks (or months) go by without a word, their silence may indicate who’s really holding this connection together.

Industry observers note that “At a minimum, a good friend (even a busy one) will periodically check in out of curiosity and interest,” Tiana Leeds, LMFT, a therapist based in Santa Barbara, California, tells SELF. After all, someone who truly cares about you should want to know what’s going on in your life, which is why if they consistently don’t try to get in touch (or only expect you to do so), they may not be genuinely interested in your world.

Venting to your friends is natural—some would even argue it can strengthen your bond. That remarked, being there for each other is supposed to be a two-way street, Hope Kelaher, LCSW, author of Here to Make Friends: How to Make Friends as an Adult, tells SELF.

If someone unloads their laundry list of problems but doesn’t listen to yours, “they’re likely using you as their on-call therapist,” Kelaher says. This one-directional dynamic could look like a person who constantly complains about their boss but changes the subject whenever you open up about your work-related stress. Or they dominate dinner conversations with their dating disasters, yet they’re “busy,” uninterested, or MIA when you need relationship advice. Over time, investing all your time and energy into people who won’t give back can drain your energy, Leeds says, and leave you feeling neglected by a person who’s supposed to have your back.

Maybe they insist on eating at restaurants near their place, which means you have to travel across town every single time. They only reach out when “better” looks fall through (“Hey, my dinner got canceled. What are you doing tonight?”), making you feel more like an afterthought than a priority. More subtly, perhaps they’re only interested in brief 15-minute coffee chats that fit their schedule instead of a dedicated dinner or movie night.

It has been revealed that “In a healthy relationship there should always be a give-and-take,” Kelaher says, meaning both people need to compromise. So it’s disheartening when, again and again, someone you’d do anything for won’t meet you halfway (sometimes literally).

Your friend might be a workaholic or chronically forgetful (which, don’t get us wrong, is still frustrating). But that alone doesn’t mean your bond is one-sided.

Instead, “consider the bigger picture and ask yourself, ‘Is their behavior a reflection of not caring about me, or just a difference in availability and communication style?’” Leeds notes. As an example, someone who takes five business days to reply to anyone’s messages may not be singling you out. What’s more telling, though, is if that same person who’s “too swamped” to text you regularly posts Instagram stories of brunches, dinners, and post-work meetups with others in their social circle. Or if your usually punctual friend (who’s known for being reliable) is comfortable canceling plans only with you. These inconsistencies, Kelaher says, suggest that they’re perfectly capable of showing up—just not for you.

According to recent reports, let’s say you mentioned how vital it would be to have support at your first 5K race. A friend who truly cares might surprise you at the finish line with flowers, or at the very least shoot over a heartfelt “Good luck!” or “Congrats!” In a one-sided friendship, however, this kind of consideration may be missing entirely. They might downplay your achievement (“Sorry I couldn’t make it, but it was such a short race!”) or forget your major day without a hint of apology.

True friends go the extra mile to celebrate your successes and be there during tough moments. That’s why if someone repeatedly forgets significant events like your birthday, or rarely indicates empathy for your challenges (like a scary medical procedure, a high-stakes presentation), they may not be as invested as they should be.

Therapists recommended bringing up your concerns non-confrontationally.

Ideally, their response can give you a glimpse into whether they’re aware of this imbalance and, more importantly, if they’re willing to work on it. That mentioned, you can’t force someone to be a good friend, so if they don’t care enough to show up for you, know that you deserve better. “After all, friendships take work, Leeds says. “But it’s not meant to be done by just one person.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Newly introduced York judge has refused to throw out a lawsuit over a 15th-century Fra Angelico painting that the heirs to the Bic pen fortune say was stolen by their family chauffeur and later sold by the late art dealer Richard Feigen.
  • In a decision dated October 26 and filed on November 16, Fresh York Supreme Court Justice James G.
  • Recent findings suggest that “No family should lose a treasured work of art simply because the people who handled this stolen property were sophisticated dealmakers,” Luke Nikas, a lawyer for the Bich family, told ARTnews.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Newly introduced York judge has refused to throw out a lawsuit over a 15th-century Fra Angelico painting that the heirs to the Bic pen fortune say was stolen by their family chauffeur and later sold by the late art dealer Richard Feigen.

In a decision dated October 26 and filed on November 16, Fresh York Supreme Court Justice James G. Clynes rejected an attempt by Feigen’s estate and associated businesses to get the case dismissed. Their main argument? The family had waited too long to sue.

Recent findings suggest that “No family should lose a treasured work of art simply because the people who handled this stolen property were sophisticated dealmakers,” Luke Nikas, a lawyer for the Bich family, told ARTnews. The Bich family is determined to recover what belongs to them, and today’s decision is an important step toward achieving that result.” The ruling is good news for the Bich heirs, though there’s still a long way to go. The judge hasn’t decided who owns the painting, or even whether it was stolen. Related Articles Adam Lindemann Sued by Nature Conservancy for Allegedly Installing Julian Schnabel Sculpture Without Permission Fra Angelico's Restored Fiesole Altarpiece Returns to Its Original Church Home After Blockbuster Museum Show.

Sources indicate that as ARTnews reported in April, the dispute centers on Saint Sixtus (ca. 1453–55), a painting by the Italian Renaissance master that Baron Marcel Bich, the founder of Bic, bought at Sotheby’s in 1972 for £130,000. The painting eventually passed to his son Bruno, who kept it in his Fifth Avenue apartment in Manhattan. Then, around 2006, it disappeared.

According to a lawsuit filed in March by Bruno’s three sons, Gonzalve, Charles, and Guillaume, the family’s chauffeur, Roy Morrow, stole the painting and sold it to Feigen for $3 million. The family claims Morrow had no paperwork proving the painting was his, but Feigen bought it anyway and promptly insured it for $8.5 million, nearly three times what he’d paid.

It has been revealed that feigen, one of Upcoming York’s best-known Old Master dealers before his death in 2021, later consigned the painting to Christie’s. In 2018, it was sold for $5.4 million to Chilean billionaire Álvaro Saieh and his wife, Ana Guzmán.

The Bich brothers say they didn’t learn where the painting ended up until 2023. They asked for it back the following year, but Saieh and Guzmán refused. So the brothers sued, demanding the painting’s return, along with damages and money from its sale.

Feigen’s representatives tell a different story. In March, lawyers for his estate told Reuters that Morrow had signed a bill of sale saying he owned the painting. The Saiehs, meanwhile, have noted they bought it in good faith, relying on Christie’s research.

Which brings us to the latest ruling.

Feigen’s lawyers argued that the family had simply waited too long to bring its claims. After all, Feigen bought the painting in 2006 and sold it in 2018. The brothers didn’t file their lawsuit until March 2026.

But stolen art can be a tricky business under New York law. Generally, when someone buys a stolen artwork in good faith, the clock doesn’t start ticking on a claim for its return until the rightful owner demands it back and the buyer refuses.

Things get more complicated when someone is accused of knowingly dealing in stolen property. The clock can start earlier, and Clynes mentioned there were too many unanswered questions about Feigen’s purchase to settle the problem now.

According to recent reports, the judge also rejected, for now, an argument that the family had dragged its feet for so long that allowing the case to continue would be unfair. Lawyers call that laches. Both arguments can come up again later.

In a recent development, feigen’s side did score one win. The judge dismissed claims against his revocable trust and its trustees because the family hadn’t shown enough to connect the trust to the money from the painting’s sale. The brothers can bring those claims again if they find more evidence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the best environmental storytelling in video games doesn’t always hit you in the face and demand you stop to look, and GTA 6 has perfected that. Sometimes it’s a carefully dressed room, an overgrown garden, or a detail you spot out of the corner of your eye while heading somewhere else.

Rockstar’s developers say that kind of discovery is central to Grand Theft Auto 6, a world designed to reward players who take their time. After three weeks of playing GTA 6, I'd say the world-building is some of the best, most detailed, and most nuanced I've experienced. It can be as small as mud on a character's trainers, a branded coffee mug, or a car decal.

It has been revealed that “The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto VI,” states Adam Cochrane, Vice President of Art: Environment. “The subtle sway of trees or bunting swaying in the wind. A puddle of bin juice around the bottom of a dumpster, or an overgrown garden in a property that is unoccupied.”.

Sources indicate that it’s the sort of detail that makes a place feel inhabited rather than assembled for a game. Cochrane points to the personalisation of homes and businesses, and the little vignettes the teams have added for players to discover. Some offer in-game rewards; others are there simply to be found.

“Then you zoom out, and you look at the sheer scale of the world, and you realise that the detail you’ve been discovering on such a small scale is quite literally everywhere across the vast landscape of this world,” he states. “Then you realise that it’s all been curated, considered, and created by a human hand, and you can’t quite believe it.”.

That thinking extends beyond what you can see. Steven Messinger, Senior Design Director: Open World, explains that Rockstar has built deep backstories for things players may only glimpse. The game’s gang compounds, for example, have a fully mapped drug network, from supply routes to street-level buyers.

“Players will only pick up on bits and pieces of this,” Messinger indicates, “but having that structure in the background as something we consistently refer to helps everything feel more real, like this big machine is always running even when players aren’t there.”.

According to recent reports, it’s a huge amount of work for details many players may miss. That’s rather the point.

Harvard GSD students propose alternatives to Trump's arch

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Images by Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation.
  • Landscape architecture students at Harvard’s Graduate School of Design have designed two proposals for Memorial Circle in Washington, DC, the site of US president Donald Trump‘s proposed triumphal arch.
  • Both designs feature expansive pools of water that cover the current vehicular roundabout at Memorial Circle, and emphasise connectivity to the city’s historic processional axis and straight sightlines to the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images by Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation.

Landscape architecture students at Harvard’s Graduate School of Design have designed two proposals for Memorial Circle in Washington, DC, the site of US president Donald Trump‘s proposed triumphal arch.

Both designs feature expansive pools of water that cover the current vehicular roundabout at Memorial Circle, and emphasise connectivity to the city’s historic processional axis and straight sightlines to the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery.

The students, Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner, worked with Washington DC non profit organisation The Cultural Landscape Foundation (TCLF) on the designs. The aim was to engage the public in the design process, as the team views the government did not properly open the arch up for review.

“By recognising Memorial Circle’s implicit expressions of monumentality, this pair of counter proposals asserts design’s capacity to critically engage history, accommodate public life, and advocate on behalf of our shared cultural landscape,” mentioned Dvorak and Geitner.

The project began after Dvork and Geitner attended a seminar at the GSD taught by TCLF founding partner Charles A Birnbaum.

“As graduate students in landscape architecture, we took Birnbaum’s course to ground our emerging practices in critical historical inquiry and public participation,” they said.

“The current administration’s assertion of authority over national memory presented an opportunity to put these convictions into practice.”.

The first proposal treats Memorial Circle as “a void along the historic axis between Washington and Arlington”. The designers chose to fill the central roundabout circle, presently covered by grass, with a low-lying pool of water.

A natural stone perimeter surrounds the pool and is inscribed with words of “belonging and unity”.

It’s design is “restrained” according to the team, and primarily meant to be viewed from a vehicle while passing through the traffic circle.

The second proposal does away with the traffic circle entirely and instead inserts a straight thoroughfare to Arlington Memorial Bridge.

Two circular fountains would be located on either side of the road. Additionally, a large pool of water, mirroring the perimeter of the former traffic circle, would fill up the site during commemorative events when the bridge is closed.

It draws upon previous historical proposals for Memorial Circle and seeks to pay homage to the precedent of the site.

“[The fountain] geometries arise from the site’s historic proposals, combining concentric circles, intersecting alignments, and formal planting into a composition that acknowledges history whilst creating its own present identity,” noted the designers.

“In this way the landscape becomes a physical record of its own change.”.

Trump’s proposed arch was announced late last year with renderings by US studio Harrison Design. It features gilded statues and a neoclassical design and has been dubbed the “Arc de Trump” – a play on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.

Construction on the arch was set to begin in September with the government barreling ahead, but it was halted in early November by Judge Tanya S Chutkan.

Trump has claimed the arch will serve as a “military complex” with snipers in an attempt to use national security as a pretext for construction.

Many take glitch with the arch blocking views to adjacent Arlington Cemetery, including members of the Kennedy family, who filed a lawsuit to block construction, claiming that the arch would cast shadows over the grave of president John F Kennedy.

The US Commission of Fine Arts (CFA), which reviews projects in the capital city, approved the project in May.

The proposals also follow recent efforts by the legislature to change Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider the impact of proposed projects on historic properties.

Earlier in November, protesters gathered in Washington DC in opposition of the administration’s proposed rewrite of these protections. They are couched within the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) bill recently introduced to Congress.

Images by Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation.

The new Grand Theft Auto arrived this week, the messianic reward after 13 long years, offering the best-rendered version of the series’ standing promise: anything, within the scope of its metropolis and the player’s imagination. I watched my cousin paint a house for his avatar’s girlfriend, then hop in a car and drive to the Bass Museum. Or rather, to the Vice City Museum of Art, the faithful replica of it in Vice City, the game’s fictional Miami.

According to recent reports, rockstar teased that Grand Theft Auto VI would boast the franchise’s sharpest graphics yet, and the claim was not exaggerated. The Vice Museum of Art captures the Bass’s signature civic Art Deco style: a pale limestone facade (the real stuff was quarried in the Florida Keys) and, as far as I could tell, even the carved decorative relief around the entry. It’s a far cry from the series’ earliest entries, when a building like this would have been a smooth beige box; here, the facade looks textured. We parked and admired its public art: a riff on Miami Mountain, a tower of boulders by Ugo Rondinone permanently installed in Collins Park, outside the Bass. Part of Rondinone’s “Mountain” series, it’s made of garishly clashing fluorescent rocks stacked high and probably visible from space. The Vice City version has swapped stone for emojis: winking, crying, smiling. Vice City may be hiding another Easter egg for art heads. It’s a safe bet that it’s a nod to Art Basel Miami Beach, held at the Miami Beach Convention Center, since it’s set in the same font as the fair’s. The herby homage was well received. “I hope he’ll be in GTA 6 having his own little art studio or something,” wrote one Reddit user. Another added, “I can’t wait to wear this shirt to Art Basel this year, if I can pull myself away from GTA6.”.

Art Basel Miami Beach runs December 4-6; keep an eye out for Art Oregano shirts. And, perhaps, as players make it further into the notoriously long game, a new version of Art Oregano may appear.

According to recent reports, I couldn’t personally verify whether the game includes a replica of the fair, with NPCs entering and exiting, as the Vice Museum did. We’d spent the momentous night mundanely, mostly comparing paint swatches. All of it in line with what viral clips suggest: the game’s characters can do drugs and rob banks—chaos, generally speaking—but we’d rather have time to drive with no destination in mind.

Before I left, my cousin regretfully canceled our intends to visit the Guggenheim on Saturday. He has to work.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Barefoot walks on the beach. A day in their favorite high heels. A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago. These are the goals—big and small—of women undergoing foot filler treatments.

Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not latest, though it is gaining in popularity. As early as the 1960s, medical-grade silicone has been used to puff up padding deflated by age, years of wear and tear, and fashionable footwear, especially high heels. All of this puts intense pressure on the balls of the feet—otherwise known as the metatarsals.

Industry observers note that over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates. Fat pad atrophy affects 30% of people over the age of 60. Without that natural cushion, the bones in your feet come into closer contact with the ground, which causes a deep bruise-like pain in the heels or balls of the feet when walking barefoot or standing for long periods.

For some perspective, look at the doughy wonders that are baby feet and compare them to yours. As we age, wear and tear breaks down that plush tissue. And if you put your feet to heavy use, you’ll wear down that cushion quicker. Some of that internal cushioning can be restored—even if just temporarily—with the injection of dermal fillers.

In a recent development, “It’s getting very popular because people are already familiar with it for aesthetic [uses],” states Ben Pearl, DPM, a podiatrist at Arlington Foot and Ankle in Arlington, Virginia. Dr. Pearl specializes in sports medicine and treats endurance athletes looking to restore cushion lost in their feet from pounding the pavement.

Patients don’t have just one choice for injectables, though. Many of the same options available for cosmetic use have also shown promise for feet. There’s hyaluronic acid filler, which adds physical volume and cushioning, and calcium hydroxylapatite, such as Radiesse, which adds firm volume while also promoting newly introduced collagen growth. Sometimes human body fat is used as the injectable, known as adipose tissue, a practice that is swiftly becoming the preferred method.

“[A fat injection] actually recruits your body to rebuild the fat pad in that area so it has a much longer duration,” states Anne Sharkey, DPM, of Soley Podiatry in Austin. Fat allografts from brands like Liposana and Leneva may last as long as two years, compared to hyaluronic acid fillers, which typically need a touch up in six to nine months.

According to recent reports, this type of regenerative medicine is appealing to patients. It’s not a promise that the foot will return to its former glory, but that it will be “as close to normal as possible,” notes Dr. Pearl.

Dr. Sharkey and Dr. Pearl have both seen positive results from their patients. Scientific studies corroborate the efficacy of the treatment as well. One small study looking at patients with metatarsal pain found five patients had no more pain six months post-hyaluronic acid injections, and those who still had pain could wear high heels twice as long as they could before the injections. Another study surveying patients who had been injected with body fat reported that their pain improved by more than 70 percent on average, 20 months post injection.

While there are a growing number of cosmetic clinics offering the procedure, Dr. Pearl cautions against allowing just any injector at it. That’s because injecting filler into feet is a more complex procedure than an aesthetic injection. For one, knowing where to inject requires an understanding of the foot’s pressure points. In his own practice, Dr. Pearl uses ultrasound to help determine where to replace the fat to offload the pain. Additionally, Dr. Pearl notes, the skin is much tougher on the feet than the face, making it a more complicated area to inject.

This is one reason why Dr. Sharkey set up her practice to include a nail salon—combining cosmetology and podiatry. Her patients are already familiar with dermal fillers. Within the attached nail salon you can get manicures, pedicures, ingrown nail treatment, toenail reconstruction, or dermal fillers for feet.

Sources indicate that try not to groan, but it depends. The cost of the procedure is influenced by how much filler is injected, and which brand is used. Other factors that affect cost include how your provider bills the procedure, and how much experience they have with dermal filler injections.

Recent findings suggest that for cosmetic use, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons places the average cost of hyaluronic acid filler treatment at $715. They estimate nonhyaluronic acid fillers, including Radiesse, Sculptra, and Liposana to cost $901 on average per treatment. However, the feet will almost certainly require more filler than the face, so you can expect the cost to be higher.

In a recent development, but will insurance cover it? Unlikely. “Even though it isn't technically cosmetic, it may not be considered medically necessary, because these procedures are often considered elective and cosmetic branding has a box drawn around it,” claims Mark Welter, chief strategy and growth officer at Welter Healthcare Partners, a healthcare business management firm.

If you’re transparent with your provider about any financial concerns you have, they can work with you to find a middle ground between pain relief and high costs. Dr. Sharkey, for example, will often offer her patients more affordable hyaluronic acid fillers as temporary pain relief until they’re ready to dive into a more expensive fat injection.

In a recent development, if injectables aren’t accessible to you, there are other ways to deal with foot pain. Here are some options, most of which require a low financial investment.

A podiatrist can help walk you through any of these options and come up with a plan to minimize your pain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

Industry observers note that A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

Recent findings suggest that from a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

It has been revealed that finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

Industry observers note that you can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Sources indicate that not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Sources indicate that communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any complications.

In a recent development, hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

In a recent development, remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that nendo has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the Dutch designer explains why she doesn’t find design inspiring.

Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.

Industry observers note that “How I think is not typical design,” she told Dezeen. “So I’m never thinking about function in the first place. The whole process is very intuitive, it’s just a cloud of connections in my head – more about concepts or stories that I want to tell rather than making a functional piece.”.

“I’ve never been so inspired by design in general,” she added. “It’s a skill that fits very well to me, but I’d rather connect it in inspiration to art, to architecture, or another discipline.”.

With a highly sculptural style, Tangelder also sometimes refers to herself as an artist – a label she says she wouldn’t have dared use when starting out.

She has made a name for herself through pieces that often play with unexpected juxtapositions of materials and use traditional methods of production to create an unmistakably contemporary aesthetic.

According to recent reports, “I like to use poor materials, rich materials, and fuse them,” she explained. “For me, it’s sort of a synonym for how I think culture should be.”.

In 2019, she was identified by Dezeen as a young designer to watch after exhibiting at Collectible, as well as winning that year’s Biennale Interieur designer of the year award.

Explaining the studio’s decision to select her as a 20×20 nomination, Nendo praised Tangelder’s approach for being “both remarkably gentle and quietly bold”.

“Driven by a playful curiosity to take architecture apart and put it back together, she reveals qualities in familiar materials that we have long overlooked,” the studio told Dezeen.

Referencing buildings in the medium of furniture has become something of a calling card for Tangelder.

Notable examples include the Bolder Chair, which recalls architectural columns, the Windows of Bo Bardi table, which mimics the shape of windows on the SESC Pompéia Factory in São Paulo, and Brick’s Reflection Chair with its terracotta backrest (pictured left).

These propensities are reflected evocatively in the name of Tangelder’s studio – Destroyers/Builders – though recently, she tends to work more under her own name.

Sources indicate that “I’m inspired by architecture, things I see in buildings,” she said. “I think it’s just really interesting to scale it down to the field of artistic design, or limited-edition design.”.

“In the history of architecture there’s so much to tell,” she continued. “For me it’s more diverse and also less superficial than the history of design, and I think that’s what interests me so much.”.

“And also that it feels more essential, I think that is maybe the core. I just like brick. I like simple materials that are used for construction rather than smooth finishes just for decoration.”.

Not that she is completely opposed to smooth, decorative finishes – as evidenced by the fact that an entire room in the home-slash-studio that she shares with her landscape-architect partner is used exclusively for lacquering.

In fact, most of the house, which is in a leafy area outside Brussels, is taken up by Tangelder’s atelier space.

She moved to Belgium shortly after graduating from Design Academy Eindhoven in 2013, and has become part of an increasingly rich design scene in the country over the past decade.

Sources indicate that in the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing. Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there’s so much investment in each project.

Recent findings suggest that “I moved to Belgium because I really like the culture, the art scene, architecture as well,” said Tangelder. “The design scene I thought was actually quite minimal, or I didn’t really see a lot of studios at that time. But I liked that as well, it felt a little bit more upcoming for me.”.

According to recent reports, “I think it developed a lot, the landscape in design in Belgium over the last 10 years,” she considered. “There’s a lot happening right now.”.

It has certainly been a productive decade for Tangelder, whose back-catalogue is impressively extensive considering she has only ever employed a very small number of assistants.

Part of that has been made possible thanks to collaborations with the healthy network of craftspeople across Belgium that Tangelder has established to help with production.

“That has been super important for me,” she noted. “Each material that I really love, I have a partner now.”.

Industry observers note that but moreover, the chunky portfolio is a reflection of a huge amount of hours spent working in the studio. Though she says her work-life balance is improving, Tangelder works almost every day including weekends, and has been known to go years without a holiday.

“I really like it, so for me it’s the best way to spend my time,” she said, before pausing.

It has been revealed that “I should think about it more as fun time, because of course it’s also a struggle. You’re always struggling over all the decisions that have to be made.”.

It has been revealed that so that means you take risks all the time. It’s maybe more intense, but also more fun.

Like many independent designers, Tangelder has had to battle to earn a living from her discipline.

“In the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing,” she remembered. “Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there’s so much investment in each project.”.

Over time, she says she has acquired a reasonably good sense of which pieces are likely to prove more lucrative, though she has resisted the temptation to focus her energies entirely on these.

“I think when you decide to only continue projects that you know will have commercial success, then it will be less experimental,” she explained.

Sources indicate that “So that means you take risks all the time,” she added. “It’s maybe more intense, but also more fun.”.

Most of Tangelder’s work involves one-off or limited-edition pieces for galleries, but she has also partnered with brands.

A big moment came in 2022 when she was commissioned by Cassina to produce a collection of side tables and pouffes, and she has continued to work with the Italian brand each year since.

This year she was able to put on a solo exhibition at Milan design week supported by Cassina, showcasing a combination of her independent pieces and products created for the brand.

Sources indicate that I just think the material is very me. That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It’s really in between a sculpture and a functional object.

It was an unusual example of small-scale making and larger-scale production design being displayed side-by-side.

Far from being a barrier to creative expression, Tangelder has found that these commissions can be an enabler by providing up-front revenues, unlike solo work.

“So it gives less pressure, I would say, which is very good for the creative process,” she said.

But you can have too much of a good thing, and while she enjoys the more collaborative experience of working for a brand she limits this type of work to two projects per year to ensure she has plenty of time for her own pieces.

According to recent reports, tangelder’s current obsession is cast and oxidised metal, so she reports spending a lot of time these days in a foundry in Antwerp. Her most recent piece is a grungy take on a conventional desk lamp, in white bronze.

“I just think the material is very me,” she remarked. “That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It’s really in between a sculpture and a functional object.”.

Looking to the future, she is interested in working more with fashion, having previously designed a chair for Dior.

And, she would like to work on a larger-scale installation – perhaps an outdoor sculpture, she suggests.

In a world where for various reasons the boundary between design and art is increasingly blurred, Tangelder is undoubtedly at the forefront.

She is an interesting 20/20 choice from Sato, who is typically associated with minimalist, highly functional product design.

For her part, Tangelder sees her work as partly an indirect response to the Sato approach – a continuation of a conversation.

“I have, of course, quite a different form language, but I think it’s also a reaction to what he’s done,” she said.

“He’s so clear in the decisions that he makes, he’s a master in it, and I’m really grateful that he sees what I’ve been doing.”.

El Greco Masterpiece Gets Its Colors Back After More Than 400 Years

💡 Key Takeaways
  • King Philip II of Spain wasn’t particularly impressed with El Greco‘s The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion when he first saw it.
  • A painstaking nine-month restoration, recently finished, has found the monumental painting looking considerably more like the one El Greco envisioned.
  • According to recent reports, the restoration was conducted at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery, under the supervision of Rafael Alonso, an 81-year-old former Prado Museum restorer, who has spent decades working on El Greco’s paintings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

King Philip II of Spain wasn’t particularly impressed with El Greco‘s The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion when he first saw it. The following four centuries of dirt, varnish, and enthusiastic repainting hadn’t done the picture any favors, either.

A painstaking nine-month restoration, recently finished, has found the monumental painting looking considerably more like the one El Greco envisioned. The muddy browns and sickly greens that had dulled the picture for generations are gone. In their place are brilliant blues, reds, yellows, and purples, along with a newfound depth that had been buried beneath grime. Related Articles AI Model Reveals New Information About Authorship of 17th-Century El Greco Altarpiece 15th-Century Bellini Altarpiece in Venice to Be Restored While the Public Watches.

According to recent reports, the restoration was conducted at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery, under the supervision of Rafael Alonso, an 81-year-old former Prado Museum restorer, who has spent decades working on El Greco’s paintings. The project was supported by the Fundacion Callia in partnership with Spain’s Patrimonio Nacional, which oversees the country’s royal collections.

According to recent reports, the results were reported in detail by El País, whose writer followed the restoration from the painting’s removal from El Escorial in February through its finished restoration in October. And what a job it was.

In a recent development, alonso had initially expected the restoration to take about four months. But once he and fellow restorer Adela Murgui began cleaning the enormous canvas, which measures nearly 15 feet high and 10 feet wide, they discovered that its condition was far worse than even feared.

“When I put the cotton to the painting, my heart sank,” Alonso told El País. Centuries of varnish and repainting had darkened the colors and flattened the composition. In the 19th century, he explained, painters had simply painted over damaged areas, often adding their own interpretations of what El Greco intended.

The restorers spent months carefully stripping away those additions, revealing the original paint beneath. Afterward, the repaired the damaged areas using soluble materials, taking pains not to add anything that couldn’t be removed later.

The restoration is particularly striking given the painting’s rather unhappy beginnings.

El Greco painted The Martyrdom between 1580 and 1582 for the basilica at El Escorial, Philip II’s vast monastery and palace outside Madrid. The king wanted a powerful statement of Catholic faith, while the artist hoped the commission might secure him a permanent position as a court painter.

Neither’s wish was totally granted.

It has been revealed that rather than concentrate on the grisly execution of Saint Maurice and his fellow Christian soldiers, El Greco pushed the violence into the background. Up front, he placed a group of handsome soldiers in brightly colored clothing, their elongated bodies and theatrical poses exemplary of the skills he had learned in Venice and Rome.

Philip II apparently admired the painting’s quality, paying the artist a substantial sum of 800 ducats, but felt it wasn’t right for its intended religious setting. The work was relegated to another room, and El Greco never clinched the royal appointment he’d hoped for.

The painting stayed there for most of the next 444 years, apart from a trip to Madrid for an exhibition in 1999, all the while gradually losing most of its remarkable color and atmosphere.

The restoration also marks another achievement for the Fundacion Callia, founded by Carmen Reviriego, which has helped restore works by Zurbarán, Rubens, Brueghel the Elder, Velázquez, and others through its partnership with Madrid’s Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando. According to El País, the foundation has helped mobilize €5 million for the preservation of artworks.

Sources indicate that when ARTnews spoke with Reviriego in March, she described Callia as an “incubator of patrons,” bringing together collectors and philanthropists from Spain, Latin America, and beyond. Her goal is to encourage a stronger culture of private support for the arts in a country that has traditionally relied heavily on public funding.

Reviriego had specifically mentioned The Martyrdom during that interview as an example of the work the foundation hoped to support. “El Greco was the Jeff Koons or Damien Hirst of his day,” she told ARTnews this week, “and Phillip II was the most power man and greatest patron of the 16th century.”.

According to recent reports, there’s a nice historical symmetry here. Reviriego argued that great works of art are rarely the achievement of an artist alone. Without patrons, many wouldn’t exist at all. She pointed to the Royal Collections themselves, built in part through the patronage of Philip II, the very king who commissioned The Martyrdom more than four centuries ago. Now, private patronage has helped give that painting a new life.

Recent findings suggest that for Alonso, meanwhile, the completed restoration marks something of a farewell. After decades spent working on El Greco’s paintings, he told El País that The Martyrdom was the last of the artist’s great masterpieces still awaiting restoration.

Industry observers note that the newly restored painting is expected to go on temporary display at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery before returning to El Escorial. This time, visitors will get a much better idea of what Philip II saw more than four centuries ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I test out the very best audiophile wired headphones for a living and out of all of them, the best open-back option is hands down the HEDDphone D1. And even at its original price of £599, it's worth every penny.

But thanks to this early Black Friday headphone deal, the HEDDphone D1 is now down from £599 to £499 over at Peter Tyson.

It has been revealed that open-back headphones are the holy grail for audiophiles craving a spacious soundstage, but they usually offer some unique hurdles to achieve true tonal accuracy. When I first heard the HEDDphone D1 last November, I said that the German audio organization had cracked the code. It's why they remain my top pick of the best-sounding wired, over-ear headphones at any price.

Industry observers note that sure, the HEDDphone D1 pack world-first driver technology and are hand-built in Germany, but for me that's not the main pull. It's the sound these things make! If you want neutral, balanced, slightly lean and mean but with exquisite detail, they're the best option at £599 – and a steal at £499!

In a recent development, if you do get the HEDDphone D1 it's worth getting a quality headphone stand too. And you really don't have to spend loads of money to get a good-quality, handsome, wooden stand. For me a good option is the Linkidea wooden stand. Even when it's not discounted, under £30 is a bargain.

Usually I don't pay the marketing hype much time, but I make an exception with the HEDDphone D1. That's because they offer the world’s first dynamic driver headphone with a Thin-Ply Carbon Diaphragm (TPCD). Developed in partnership with Swedish material specialists Composite Sound, this aerospace-grade tech controls resonance structurally, eliminating the need for normal driver damping (and the compromises that that method invariably brings). What that all means for me and you is fast transients, and excellent clarity. These things are detailed!

At 350g, they are lightweight for this tier of headphone – audiophile headphones can get heavy at around the £500 mark. With an impedance of 32ohms and 100dB sensitivity, they're easy to drive – including with inexpensive dongle DACs.

This is a genuinely special headphone, and a decent Black Friday price.

#125824. The 16 Most Expensive Artworks Ever Sold at Auction

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4235 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Artnews ↗ Open Full Page

The 16 Most Expensive Artworks Ever Sold at Auction

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Auction records make for great headlines, like the 2026 banner sale of Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which topped $236.4 million at Sotheby’s.
  • According to recent reports, look at the list of the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, and you’ll see more than just a parade of billionaires with good taste (or at least expensive taste).
  • Yes, Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million, but is it really a Leonardo?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Auction records make for great headlines, like the 2026 banner sale of Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which topped $236.4 million at Sotheby’s. There’s a thrill in watching numbers climb into the stratosphere, each sale another reminder that, in the art market, money has a way of bending reality. But the price of a painting has never been the most interesting thing about it.

According to recent reports, look at the list of the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, and you’ll see more than just a parade of billionaires with good taste (or at least expensive taste). You’ll see a history of ideas—what mattered to the artists who made them, what obsessed the collectors who chased them, and how we decide, decades or centuries later, which works still hold power.

Yes, Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million, but is it really a Leonardo? Picasso’s Women of Algiers, Pollock’s Number 7A, 1948, and Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn all shattered records, with the Pollock work shooting far beyond its $100 million estimate when it came to auction at Christie’s in May 2026 in a sale of works from the S. I. Newhouse collection. But these works’ real value has nothing to do with what someone was willing to pay on a given evening at Christie’s. The best art—the kind that shifts culture, lingers in your mind, and changes how you see the world—exists in a space money can’t touch.

Industry observers note that but of course, once a work crosses a threshold, there’s something almost inevitable about the price spiral. With each record-breaking sale, the bar gets set higher, the stakes get sharper, and the frenzy deepens. The game has changed, but in a way, the auction houses are just as much a stage for the spectacle as for the art itself. Every price tag opens the door to another possibility. If one work can sell for $450 million, what’s to stop the next from reaching half a billion—or more? With so many players in the game, all vying for the ultimate cultural trophy, the numbers have a way of multiplying faster than the logic behind them.

And yet, the more those numbers rise, the further they drift from the essential thing that makes art so valuable: the art itself. High prices can make us think we’re in the presence of something transcendent, but it’s the work that holds the power, not the price. So, here’s the list. The numbers are staggering, but don’t get too caught up in them. The real story is in the art itself.

In a recent development, A version of this article was first published on November 19, 2025. It was last updated on November 20, 2026.

Sold for $119.9 million at Sotheby’s New York in May 2012.

When it sold for $107 million at Sotheby’s New York, Munch’s pastel The Scream (1895), one of the four versions—two painted and two in pastel—that he made of the same subject, became the most expensive work ever to be sold at a public auction, stealing the trophy from Picasso’s 1932 Nude, Green Leaves and Bust, which sold at Christie’s in 2010 for $106.5 million.

At the time, it was the only version of The Scream still in private hands; its seller was Petter Olsen, a Norwegian businessman whose father, Thomas, was Munch’s friend and patron. The picture, which opened at $40 million, sparked a 12-minute bidding war, with wide-eyed potential buyers both in the salesroom and on the phones. According to the Wall Street Journal, its buyer was investor Leon Black, a trustee at the Museum of Modern Art, where The Scream later went on view.

After the sale Olsen, described by Art in America as “the wild-haired and bespectacled seller,” read a statement that tied the work to climate change and global warming: “The Scream for me shows the horrifying moment when man realizes his impact on nature and the irreversible changes that he has initiated, making the planet increasingly uninhabitable. . . . More death, less life. And very few lifeboats left as we go down.”.

Sold for $121 million at Christie’s Latest York in November 2024.

Sources indicate that the “crown jewel” of the auction market in 2024 (as Christie’s so humbly put it) was perhaps the finest example of a subject that Magritte revisited more than 25 times throughout his career: an otherworldly scene showing a house on tree-lined street at night. But instead being enveloped in darkness, the sky above the trees is impossibly blue, with massive, cottony clouds floating by. This 1954 version of Empire of Light, which sold for $121 million and came from the collection of designer and philanthropist Mica Ertegun, set a new record for Magritte’s work at auction.

Sources indicate that after the sale, Christie’s chairman of 20th and 21st century art Alex Rotter said the house that evening had adopted a “masterpiece approach” to this sale. “In a market that is not so easy to maneuver, we thought that if we present the greatest works we can get … these are the best examples,” Rotter said, admitting that the auction had its share of lots that didn’t catch collectors’ attention. But “the works that we put all the emphasis behind really proved us right. They had multiple bidders and indicated that a market based on individual taste is on the rise.”.

Sold for $137.7 million at Christie’s New York in November 2022.

In a recent development, cézanne’s deliciously rich landscape of the French countryside and his beloved Mont Sainte-Victoire is the second of five works from the Paul Allen sale at Christie’s to make this list. When the hammer fell, Mont Sainte-Victoire (1888–90) doubled Cézanne’s previous auction high of $60.5 million, for a still life from the collection of John Hay Whitney.

Like Cézanne’s best works, Mont Sainte-Victoire breaks aspects of the world—in this case, a French mountain—into shapes shaded with color, as though they were three-dimensional geometrical forms. In that way, Cézanne paved the way for Cubist artists such as Pablo Picasso and George Braque, who would push his innovations even further toward abstraction.

Sold for $139.3 million at Sotheby’s New York in November 2023.

According to recent reports, woman with a Watch (1932), one of Picasso’s many paintings of his mistress Marie-Thérèse Walter, became the second most expensive work by the artist ever sold at auction when it fetched $139 million at Sotheby’s in 2023. The canvas, from the collection of late philanthropist Emily Fisher Landau, drew intense bidding before selling to a phone bidder represented by Sotheby’s head of global fine art, Brooke Lampley.

It has been revealed that woman with a Watch had a rarefied provenance, changing hands just a few times since Picasso painted it in 1932. It was acquired by Landau in 1968 from Pace Gallery, which had purchased it from Switzerland’s Galerie Beyeler two years earlier.

In a recent development, pictures of Walter typically go for top dollar. In 2010, Nude, Green Leaves and Bust—also painted in 1932—broke records at $106.5 million. Still, the most expensive Picasso of all time is a work that does not depict Walter. But more on that in a bit.

Sold for $140.8 million at Poly International Auction Co., Ltd., Beijing in December 2017.

Sources indicate that qi Baishi’s Twelve Screens of Landscapes (1925) shattered records in 2017, selling for RMB 931.5 million ($140.8 million) at Beijing Poly Auction and making it the most expensive Chinese artwork ever sold at auction. The bidding war lasted over 20 minutes, with more than 60 bid increments before a Chinese collector secured the 12-panel piece.

Each 70-inch panel captures a sweeping vista from Qi’s travels across China. Originally displayed at his solo exhibition in 1954 and later featured in a memorial show in 1958, the set of panels was kept by Qi’s pupil, Xiuyi Guo, before resurfacing at auction.

Sources indicate that A similar version of Twelve Screens of Landscapes, painted around 1932 as a gift to Kuomintang general Wang Zuanxu, resides in the Chongqing Museum. The set sold in 2017 was the only one in private hands at the time, making it a rarity.

Sold for $141.3 million at Christie’s New York in May 2015.

Alberto Giacometti’s Pointing Man (1947) became the most expensive sculpture ever sold at auction when it fetched $141.3 million at Christie’s Newly introduced York in May 2015. The life-size bronze, standing at more than five and a half feet tall, was sold by real estate magnate Sheldon Solow, surpassing Giacometti’s previous auction record of $104.3 million, which was set at Sotheby’s London five years earlier by Walking Man I (1960).

One of six casts made by the artist (not counting an additional artist’s proof), this particular Pointing Man had been held privately for 45 years before the sale. Four of those casts reside in major museums, including the Museum of Modern Art in Upcoming York and the Tate in London, which made this auction a prime opportunity for collectors. Similar sculptures by Giacometti depicting skeletal, elongated figures have likewise sold for significant sums.

At the time, Christie’s head Pylkkänen called the piece “one of the finest works of art I have had the honor to handle.” Whoever bought the piece clearly agreed about its quality.

Sold for $142.4 million at Christie’s Fresh York in November 2013.

Francis Bacon’s Three Studies of Lucian Freud (1969) briefly became the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction when it sold for $142.4 million at Christie’s Upcoming York in November 2013. The triptych surpassed the previous record, held by Edvard Munch’s pastel The Scream, which sold for $119.9 million at Sotheby’s in 2012 (and which also appears on this list, above).

It has been revealed that bacon’s three-panel portrait—each part stands six and a half feet tall—depicts Bacon’s longtime friend and artistic rival, Lucian Freud, in a series of contorted poses. The piece had an unusual history: its panels were separated by a dealer in the 1970s and remained apart for 15 years before being reunited by a collector in 1989.

According to recent reports, the work was expected to sell for over $85 million, but after a five-minute bidding war, it was secured by Latest York’s Acquavella Galleries. In a strategic move, Christie’s shifted the Bacon painting to the ninth lot of the evening to allow unsuccessful bidders a chance at other works—an approach that proved successful, contributing to the auction house’s record-breaking $691.6 million total for the night.

Shortly after the sale, the anonymous buyer lent the triptych to the Portland Art Museum for public viewing from December 2013 to March 2014.

Sold for $149 million at Christie’s New York in November 2022.

Sources indicate that in November 2022, an early 20th-century masterpiece by Georges Seurat, Models (Small Version) (1888), sold for a staggering $149 million at Christie’s Latest York. The painting, depicting three nude figures in Seurat’s signature pointillist style, was one of the rarest privately-owned works by the artist. It came from the collection of Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen and was expected to surpass $100 million at auction.

The bidding opened at $75 million, drawing competition from four bidders, including specialists representing clients in Latest York and Asia. After several minutes of heated back-and-forth, the work hammered at $130 million, with Christie’s Asia chairman securing the piece for a final total of $149 million, including fees. The sale set a new auction record for Seurat, shattering his previous high of $34 million, achieved in 2018 for The Harbor at Grandcamp(1885).

It has been revealed that the last time Models (Small Version) appeared on the market was in 1970, when it fetched just over $1 million at Christie’s. Prior to Allen’s ownership, it had belonged to the influential collector John Quinn, a champion of modernist artists in the early 20th century.

Sold for $157.2 million at Sotheby’s New York in May 2018.

Amedeo Modigliani’s Reclining Nude (on Her Left Side) (1917), one of the artist’s most celebrated nudes, sold for $157.2 million at Sotheby’s New York in 2018. The total price, including the buyer’s premium, followed a hammer bid of $139 million, which fell just short of its undisclosed estimate of $150 million. Despite this, the sale set a record for the most expensive artwork ever sold at Sotheby’s at the time.

According to recent reports, the large-scale canvas—depicting a nude woman gazing over her shoulder at the viewer—was the star lot of the auction house’s Impressionist and Modern art sale. Bidding opened at $125 million with auctioneer Helena Newman presiding over the room. The winning bid came from a client on the phone with Simon Shaw, Sotheby’s co-head of Impressionist and Modern art worldwide, after a subdued and measured exchange.

According to recent reports, the work belongs to Modigliani’s groundbreaking series of reclining nudes, painted between 1916 and 1919. When first exhibited in 1917 at Parisian dealer Berthe Weill’s gallery, these erotic paintings caused such a scandal that police shut down the show after just two days. At the time, only two drawings were sold.

While the sale price was extraordinary, it did not surpass Modigliani’s auction record, which remains with Reclining Nude (1917–18), sold at Christie’s in 2015 for $170.4 million to Chinese collector Liu Yiqian. Sotheby’s, however, positioned Reclining Nude (on Her Left Side) as a transformative work, with Simon Shaw stating, “There is the nude before Modigliani, and there is the nude after Modigliani.”.

Sold for $170.4 million at Christie’s New York in November 2015.

Amedeo Modigliani’s Reclining Nude (1917–18) shattered expectations at Christie’s New York in 2015, selling for $170.4 million, more than doubling the artist’s previous auction record of $70.7 million. The work, which carried an on-request estimate of over $100 million, became the second-most expensive painting ever sold at auction at the time.

The sale took place during Christie’s curated evening auction, “The Artist’s Muse,” which aimed to build buzz around 20th-century masterpieces. Despite a mixed night—with several major lots, including works by Willem de Kooning and Lucian Freud, failing to sell—the Modigliani nude electrified the room. Bidding was fierce, ultimately concluding with a Chinese collector securing the work via telephone, as revealed by Pylkkänen after the sale. (The collector was later revealed to be Chinese billionaire businessman Liu Yiqian.).

Reclining Nude is part of Modigliani’s celebrated series of reclining nudes, painted between 1916 and 1919. These works, revolutionary in their sensuality and bold in their approach to form, scandalized Paris when first exhibited at Berthe Weill’s gallery in 1917, leading to the show’s abrupt closure by police. Today, they are considered among the most important contributions to the modern nude tradition.

The sale of Reclining Nude was a high point in an otherwise uneven auction, which totaled $491.4 million—above its $440 million low estimate but falling far short of the $705.8 million brought in by a similar sale earlier that year. While other records were set that night—including for works by Gustave Courbet, Balthus, and Roy Lichtenstein—the Modigliani painting stood out as the undeniable star of the evening, solidifying the artist’s status as one of the most sought-after names in the art market.

Sold for $179.4 million at Christie’s Latest York in May 2015.

Recent findings suggest that pablo Picasso’s Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’) (1955) set a fresh auction record in 2015 when it sold for $179.4 million at Christie’s New York, becoming the most expensive painting ever sold at auction at the time. The painting, the final and most intricate piece in Picasso’s 15-work “Women of Algiers” series (1954–55), had an on-request estimate of around $140 million but soared past that figure after deep bidding.

It has been revealed that the competition for the masterpiece played out entirely over the phone, with then-Christie’s executives Loic Gouzer and Brett Gorvy representing rival bidders. Pylkkänen, serving as auctioneer, declared “Still many people in the game” as bidding climbed past $140 million. Eventually, Gorvy’s bidder emerged victorious with a hammer price of $160 million, drawing cheers from the audience.

Sources indicate that the “Women of Algiers” series was inspired by Eugène Delacroix’s 1834 masterpiece of the same name. Created in response to the Nationalist uprising in Algeria against French colonial rule, the series reflects Picasso’s fascination with both European Orientalist art and the evolving political landscape of the time. The version here is considered the most elaborate and fully realized of the set.

The painting had a notable provenance, originally acquired by Fresh York collectors Victor and Sally Ganz directly from legendary dealer Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler in 1956. It first appeared at auction in 1997, when it sold for $31.9 million—meaning its value increased nearly sixfold in less than two decades.

While Christie’s maintained confidentiality regarding the winning bidder, reports later suggested that the buyer was former Qatari Prime Minister Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani. The sale reinforced Picasso’s dominance in the art market, cementing Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’) as one of the defining auction moments of the decade.

Sold for $181.2 million at Christie’s New York in May 2026.

It has been revealed that this 11-foot-wide painting by Jackson Pollock came to auction at Christie’s with both a first-class provenance and remarkable historical cachet. Pollock painted the work in 1948, the year after he first devised his drip painting technique, in which the artist flung his paint at the canvas rather than applying it directly using his brush. The technique distanced Pollock’s hand from his painting, leaving the application of his paint to chance.

Before he owned Sotheby’s, businessman A. Alfred Taubman owned the painting, selling it to publishing magnate S. I. Newhouse in 2000. In 2026, nearly a decade after Newhouse’s death, the painting headed to sale at Christie’s with a $100 million estimate, poising it to break Pollock’s record. At the time of the Christie’s auction, the painting hadn’t been seen publicly since 1977.

Recent findings suggest that the work ended up shooting far beyond its estimate and becoming one of the most expensive paintings ever sold. Bidding opened at $80 million, and following 60 bids, the painting hammered at $157 million. With fees, the total rose to $181.2 million.

In a recent development, on November 18, 2026, Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), a picture of sunlit trees set against oncoming storm clouds, sold for $190.4 million (including fees) at Sotheby’s. The cover lot for the auction house’s Blaquier-Arrieta collection sale, which the house had billed as “legendary,” it set a new auction record for the Dutch painter. The reported buyer was dealer William Acquavella.

Recent findings suggest that the artist’s previous record of $117.2 million was set at Christie’s in November 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888), a landscape from the collection of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen, sold for $102 million. The upcoming result beat that by $73.2 million, a jump of 62.4 percent in just four years.

Sources indicate that that the sale happened at all was a victory for Sotheby’s. Just days before the auction, descendants of Samuel Fischer, the German Jewish publisher who once owned the painting, challenged its sale, arguing that their family had been forced to part with it in Amsterdam in 1936 because of Nazi persecution. Sotheby’s disputed the claim, pointing to archival records showing the painting had sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, around $22,000 at the time, which it considered a fair market price. After several days of talks, the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the Fischer heirs reached an agreement, clearing the painting’s title.

According to recent reports, painted shortly after Van Gogh arrived at Auvers-sur-Oise in May 1890, Blossoming Chestnut Trees is among the 70-plus paintings (and more than 50 drawings) that the artist made there before taking his own life only two months later. It was also one of only eight Auvers landscapes still in private hands, according to research cited by the Art Newspaper.

The electric scene, with its thick brushwork, also hadn’t been seen in decades. It was last exhibited at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in 1964 before Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro and Nelly Arrieta Blaquier, bought it in 1975—the kind of provenance and scarcity that fuels record-breaking prices like this one.—Daniel Cassady.

Sold for $195 million at Christie’s Latest York in May 2022.

Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn, one of the most iconic images in modern art, became the most expensive 20th-century artwork ever sold at auction when it fetched $195 million at Christie’s New York in 2022. The silkscreen portrait, based on a publicity still of Marilyn Monroe from the 1953 film Niagara, is part of Warhol’s famous “Shot Marilyn” series—named after a 1964 incident when performance artist Dorothy Podber fired a gun at a stack of Warhol’s canvases.

The work was the star lot of the evening, drawing competition from four bidders, including three on the phone and one in the room. Art dealer Larry Gagosian, bidding in person, ultimately secured the painting with a hammer price of $170 million, well below its $200 million estimate.

According to recent reports, the “Shot Marilyn” works are among Warhol’s most coveted pieces, with only five versions in existence. This particular portrait had been in a private collection for five decades, coming from the estate of Swiss dealers Thomas and Doris Ammann. With no financial guarantee, its sale marked a major moment for both the Warhol market and the broader contemporary art market.

In a recent development, in surpassing the $179.4 million record set by Picasso’s Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’) (1955) in 2015, Shot Sage Blue Marilyn reaffirmed Warhol’s place at the pinnacle of modern art valuations. While some experts saw the sale as a watershed moment, others noted that privately brokered transactions for blue-chip artworks have long exceeded the $200 million mark.

Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16) became the second-most expensive artwork ever sold at auction when it achieved $236.4 million at Sotheby’s in November 2025, surpassing Klimt’s previous records and setting a upcoming high for any work of modern art. The full-length portrait, one of only two named Klimt commissions in private hands, was the undisputed centerpiece of the sale of the Leonard A. Lauder Collection.

Bidding opened at $130 million and unfolded over 20 tense minutes, narrowing to two phone bidders represented by Sotheby’s specialists David Galperin and Julian Dawes. Dawes’s bidder ultimately won with a hammer price of $205 million, prompting applause in the salesroom and marking the most expensive lot ever handled by Sotheby’s. The result vaulted past Picasso’s Les Femmes d’Alger (Version ‘O’), which had held the record for a modern artwork at $179.4 million since 2015. Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn, meanwhile, made global headlines when it skirted the $200 million mark in 2022.

It has been revealed that the painting was commissioned by one of Klimt’s most vital patron families, survived wartime confiscation, and was restituted in 1948 before entering Lauder’s collection in the 1980s. Estimated in excess of $150 million, it had been widely expected to challenge the artist’s previous high. Instead, it rewrote the record books—cementing Klimt as one of the few early-modern painters consistently capable of commanding nine-figure prices in today’s market, and potentially opening the door for even more masterpieces to break the $200 million barrier.

Sold for $450.3 million at Christie’s New York in November 2017.

Industry observers note that in a landmark moment in the art world, Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi (c. 1500) set a fresh record for the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction, fetching an astonishing $450.3 million at Christie’s in New York in November 2017. The sale, which took place in a packed salesroom at Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, was driven by an intense 19-minute bidding war.

It has been revealed that bidding began in earnest at $100 million—which was also the guarantee—and escalated rapidly from there, with cheers and applause breaking out as the painting crossed the $200 million threshold. Pylkkanen, again serving as auctioneer, skillfully kept the crowd engaged as bids climbed incrementally in the final moments. At one point, the bidding reached $350 million, before finally settling at $400 million, with an additional $50 million in fees for the buyer.

According to recent reports, the Salvator Mundi’s journey to the auction block was filled with intrigue, including debates over its authenticity and a controversial restoration by conservator Dianne Modestini. Despite these uncertainties, the painting’s remarkable backstory and its connection to Leonardo da Vinci—whether authentic or not—captivated buyers. The work had once sold for just $1,175 in 2005, when it was attributed to a follower of Leonardo, but was later restored and re-attributed to the master himself.

The sale marked a culmination of a carefully orchestrated marketing campaign by Christie’s, which included a global tour and celebrity endorsements, such as Patti Smith and Leonardo DiCaprio. The Salvator Mundi’s latest auction price far eclipsed the previous record-holder, Pablo Picasso’s Women of Algiers (Version O) (1955), which had sold for $179 million earlier that year.

This sale marked not only a record-breaking moment for the auction house but also highlighted the increasingly influential role of market value in the art world, where the price tag may overshadow the painting’s historical and artistic significance.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That noted, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.
