💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler.
  • The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.
  • “I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler. In this interview, we learn why the design duo deliberately play into stereotypes.

The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.

“I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.

Josefin Zachrisson and Mira Bergh run multidisciplinary studio Swedish Girls between Stockholm and Milan, creating furniture, installations and set design.

Sources indicate that the duo met during their studies at Sweden’s Beckmans College of Design, where they graduated in 2019. They bonded over a desire to make work “without hierarchies” and maintain creative control of the studio’s output, which they prefer to call their ever-expanding “universe”.

The Big Bang for Swedish Girls was the selection of their collective’s tongue-in-cheek name, chosen after their first exhibition outing at Milan design week.

For experimental platform Alcova in 2021, Zachrisson and Bergh unveiled their ongoing metal rod Seats System project (pictured left).

Originally a single piece of modular seating without a defined front or back, the project has evolved into more metal pieces that follow the same design language, including a fruit bowl and a candle holder.

“We overheard people talking about our furniture, asking who made it, and others were like, ‘ah, it was those Swedish girls’, and we felt a bit belittled by it,” recalled Zachrisson. The duo had previously made work under their own names.

“The Swedish girl has obviously become a phenomenon,” added Bergh. “You know, blonde, sexy. But when we were talking about it, we also found it really funny because it’s so stereotypical. We thought we’d call ourselves Swedish Girls because everybody else was already calling us that.”.

It has been revealed that humour is intrinsic to Zachrisson and Bergh’s interdisciplinary practice. Even their website, admired by Marcelis, was playfully designed as a Swedish Girls-branded Google search engine. It is meant to look like the internet itself, complete with mock web pages listing each of the collective’s projects.

“We got the idea when we released the name Swedish Girls,” the pair explained.

“A professor from Beckmans called and said that we should change our name because when she Googled ‘Swedish Girls’, the search result was not exactly art and design,” they added.

“We thought that was so funny and decided to make Google about us instead of changing our name.”.

Another of the duo’s wit-inflected projects is Only Fans, an installation presented at Gothenburg’s Röhsska design museum in 2024 during local music festival Way Out West.

Dubbed “a multidimensional art experience about fan culture” in all its forms, the installation included 25 electric fans, selected as a riff on adult content platform OnlyFans, where women are often the subject of scrutiny.

“The installation was interactive, so that visitors could stand in the middle of the fans in a hysterical storm,” mentioned Bergh.

Industry observers note that our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things. But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life.

Alongside the fans, the collective presented seven laser-cut steel chairs emblazoned with I <3 Swedish Girls, along with a fanzine and female mannequins wearing “metal merch” designed by Zachrisson and Bergh.

“Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things,” considered Zachrisson.

“But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life,” she continued. “It feels like a way to approach it that makes it accessible.”.

Sources indicate that “Sometimes it’s hard because we get these questions like, ‘are you a feminist?'” added the designer. “But it’s inherently political to be a woman moving through the world. Our work is just reacting to our reality.”.

The pair is keen to highlight that although they make furniture, “social values are always a starting point” for their projects.

“We really want to have a practice that feels purposeful,” noted Zachrisson, considering the significance of partnering with institutions like design museums.

“We’ve realised that showing work in public spaces is the most key thing,” she continued.

It has been revealed that “Especially because the materials and processes we use have become quite expensive. So we want to put our pieces in public spaces so that everyone can take part in some way.”.

“You meet all different kinds of people, and we talk to them and grow from it,” added Bergh.

It has been revealed that the hardest thing is to earn money. We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money.

Despite Swedish Girls’ various collaborations and recurring presence at Milan design week, seven years after leaving Beckmans, Bergh and Zachrisson continue to work in cafes and supermarkets to fund their design practice.

The duo are hyperaware of the difficulties faced by emerging creatives, especially those like themselves who, as they put it, “want to listen to your gut and be close to the process”.

“The hardest thing is to earn money,” remarked Bergh. “We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money on very quick timelines. I feel like we should have more respect.”.

According to recent reports, “You don’t get paid in a way where you as two people can survive,” added Zachrisson. “But all these years of working and keeping our creative integrity is paying off in every way except financially.”.

When it comes to building their studio, the designers consider themselves to be playing the long game.

“Long term, it’s an investment to do it this way because we have now created a context where we can feel freedom and gain respect, which is why we were so happy when Sabine nominated us,” said Zachrisson.

“You can measure success in so many different ways and with this we feel respected, and that is so valuable.”.

The duo remarked funding that they won from Sweden’s Konstnärsnämnden arts council after graduating gave them a significant leg up when they were just starting out.

Zachrisson and Bergh are concerned that scholarships like theirs have been scarcer across Sweden in recent years thanks to the country’s right-wing administration, which came into power in 2022 and has only just been voted out of office.

According to recent reports, “All the artists we have talked to have felt an extreme difference in that time,” noted Zachrisson. “The share of the total budget allocated to culture has not been this low in 26 years.”.

Still, the pair are confident and excited about what’s to come.

“It comes in handy that we have a broad practice,” remarked Bergh. “We have prepares for the future to make it easier for ourselves to be designers.”.

In a recent development, “I like how they surprise with their projects and feel like we have only seen chapter one of their story,” concluded Marcelis. “And I can’t wait to discover the next chapter.”.

How to paint anything more easily by splitting up shapes

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2123 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that hi, my name is Petter Faustino and I spend a lot of time painting digitally.
  • Recent findings suggest that painting landscapes is fun, but they usually contain a lot of stuff to keep track of and it’s easy to lose control over a landscape.
  • It has been revealed that I’ve found that simple shapes rapidly turn into complex objects, so I like to figure out the major shapes first before I move on to smaller details.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hi, my name is Petter Faustino and I spend a lot of time painting digitally. In this workshop, I will show you a few of the ideas I like to remind myself of while I paint. I know variations of these tips have been told many times before, but sometimes you need to hear it in a specific way from a specific person in order for it to stick. I hope it helps you to improve your workflow and results.

Recent findings suggest that painting landscapes is fun, but they usually contain a lot of stuff to keep track of and it’s easy to lose control over a landscape. There are a lot of rules and principles that build on each other, and being able to recognise and find the weak links in your paintings can save a lot of time. I like to work step by step, and I usually try to focus on a couple of things at a time.

It has been revealed that I’ve found that simple shapes rapidly turn into complex objects, so I like to figure out the major shapes first before I move on to smaller details. There are of course many ways in which to paint, and sometimes you just need to let loose and paint more chaotically, but for me these tips and tricks still work as an overall guide to maintain structure and readability.

If you need the tools to get started, see our guides of the best drawing tablets and the best laptops for drawing. We also have a guide to choosing the best digital art software.

I usually think of forms in paintings as either lying down or standing: e.g., grass lying on the ground vs stone walls that stand up. It is a simplified way of thinking about angles and light, because the ground plane is often more perpendicular to the sun/main light source, and receives more light. Splitting between horizontals and verticals also informs so much more.

For instance, most things grow on the horizontal plane, verticals often cast shadows and they create overlaps. I find that thinking this way gives me a nice start to a painting, creates a natural balance and simplifies a lot of the difficulties with light and colour.

Something about big, bold shadow shapes makes the painting process feel a lot more manageable to me. Usually the shadow will play a major part in establishing form and value, but it really shines as a tool for guiding the eye and framing the composition. Dividing the image in two pushes the areas covered in shadow back and allows me to focus my attention on details in the light.

In a recent development, I like to keep things simple, and I usually try to build my images up slowly, bit by bit. I’ll start with two or three different elements, significant simple shapes in atmospheric perspective, that I split into horizontals and verticals. Then I split those shapes again into light and dark.

Industry observers note that this is usually more than enough for me to keep up with and organise early on. Once I feel like the perspective and values are working, I start adding in details, playing with the surfaces, putting in more stuff.

I’ve done a lot of art studies focusing on limited greyscale palettes (three to five tones). This has helped me a lot in both simplifying images and understanding compositions. I think of values like a chessboard: values have to be different enough so shapes stand apart, and the shapes standing apart are contrasted with shapes blending. You push and pull to amplify and obscure. Exaggerating values and pushing a graphical read helps me to keep it simple and focus on big shapes. It also helps me to control overall readability, and allows me to push storytelling by enhancing focal points.

In a recent development, I like to use diagonals in my compositions because they are very effective in guiding the eye. Placing a focal point at the end of a diagonal shape is a very simple and effective way of presenting something. I also very much enjoy slow-rising clouds in the background to indicate some movement, which again adds a bit of life into a painting. Little birds or leaves in the wind are other small details that can make a massive difference in giving a painting some life and movement.

Industry observers note that I’m very fond of brush marks that amplify the shapes they are describing, even better if the brush marks also help guide the eye. Adding details on a flat surface is hard, but you can usually apply patches of dirt and scratches on nearly anything. If you apply marks that follow the established perspective, you are boosting the volume and structure in your paintings significantly. By using value shifts and clever placement, you can also guide the eye through the planes in your painting as you see fit.

When working with value, understanding how to highlight areas with contrast is one side of the coin. The other side is understanding how to add structure and detail in areas with low contrast, outside of your areas of interest. When working on structure and detail, in an area cast in shadow or far away in the distance, I use values that are very similar in tone. I think of these ‘low interest’ areas as having their own very compressed value palette. I find that simplified marks allow the details to still be visible, but because of their compressed value range they don’t conflict with the composition or areas of interest.

According to recent reports, I think environments are a lot of fun when you can stare at them and imagine yourself or a character moving through them. The longer I am looking at a painting, the more I imagine smells, sounds and music. So because I enjoy this in other people’s work, I try to replicate it in my own. I try to make pathways that follow some sort of plan or logic, I add in multiple pathways that go in different directions, and I try to make long view distances so that people can stay a while and hopefully imagine little adventures while they look.

Overlapping is the environment artist’s best friend. It is as effective in primary school as it is in the world of professional illustration. It creates abundance and space, and it does so fairly cheaply, without all the requirements of other techniques. Paired together with atmospheric perspective, it is incredibly effective, and a lot of fun.

To keep things simple in my head, I try to break objects down into geometric shapes when I am painting. This sometimes leads to the painting actually looking very complicated, which is a nice bonus. The first order is to simplify the overall shapes into mixes of cylinders, pyramids, boxes and spheres. But after this, I like to break down surfaces themselves into triangles and mixes of squares. I like triangles a lot because I think they are very effective at indicating different angles in a plane, and they pair very well together. Layering surfaces in squares makes me feel like I’m making a grid, and while that can be great in certain environments, I often prefer triangles for breaking down more complicated, organic surfaces.

Sources indicate that ‘Pinched shadows’ is a phrase I use to describe shadow in corners, cracks and other tight spaces light is struggling to reach. It is more commonly referred to as ‘occluded shadows’, but I find that to be a very wide category so I’ve narrowed this down for myself, to specify something that is very handy for definition and structure. Shadows are a sliding scale of less light, but we often think of them as something opposite of light.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Occluded shadows’ is often used to describe details in areas cast in shadow, but I apply my pinches in the light areas as well. Corners often need a little punch, particularly if the perspective is not indicating the form on its own. I’ll use a slightly darker tone to pinch out intersections in corners and smaller details.

According to recent reports, it was a significant revelation to me when I learned how much grey is used in a lot of paintings I thought of as very colourful. Left with a strong impression of the colours that were built up to shine, I didn’t really register all the desaturated colours surrounding them. I find now when using this myself that the palette is a lot easier to control for me as well, because I get a wide spectrum using a small palette. I enjoy splitting things, and I often split my colour palette in two early on, but by blending in grey or applying it directly, I often feel like I have more than enough tones to structure my painting around.

Industry observers note that characters often tell a story simply by existing in a painting, but if you can have them interact with something or someone, they very quickly bring the world in your paintings to life. There have been a lot of jokes made on behalf of the famous stick-man and his adventures through concept art, but I do not think we should cast him aside.

According to recent reports, just because something is simple does not mean it is any less effective, and simply by existing he does bring a certain abstract story with him. He also brings a sense of scale, which is great.

Reference is awesome and you should use it, but when slotting things into a landscape, simply using reference can be a detour through a lot of pain and suffering. I often need to familiarise myself a little with the general structure if I am painting something very new. Say you want to put a giant pit next to the character in your painting, but you are unfamiliar with painting pits.

Painting straight from reference, unless you are very comfortable with perspective and volume, can feel very clunky. Controlling the light and value so that they match the scene you already have can be very difficult. In these cases, I highly recommend painting a couple of quick studies and then coming back to the painting and reference after.

Even if you are specialising in environments, I think you should try to study some anatomy as well. I think the more different stuff you paint, the easier it is to build an overall understanding for forms in general, and there are some unexpected crossovers between anatomy and environments.

Sources indicate that ears, for example, can be a great shape for designing unique canyons or spooky sci-fi worlds. They are relatively unique, however, and unless you have that shape catalogued in the back of your mind from previous studies, you might be missing out on a pretty interesting volume structure.

Starting with a basic shape, add details, separation and shadow.

For a substantial shape, I prefer the lasso tool initially, but a flat hard-edged brush is nice for touch-ups after the initial fill-in. Sometimes it’s nice to have a rough sketch to base the shape on, but you can also add lines over the shape after it is placed, and let the shape influence and limit the sketch.

In a recent development, here we separate the verticals from horizontals. You can work dark to light, or light to dark, but the trick is to get a good separation between surfaces. You also have to think big and simple: this isn’t super-strict, particularly if it’s an organic shape. Organise your landscape into these two categories.

It has been revealed that to solidify the structure, we indicate a light direction and punch out intersections and corners with pinched shadows. We also introduce diagonal surfaces between the horizontals and verticals. At this point, the structure is starting to take form. Smaller details added will follow the same rules.

Breaking: Incline Walking vs. Running: What’s the Better Workout?

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity.
  • Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.
  • At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity. But in reality, they’re both effective cardio options that challenge your body in distinct ways—from the muscles you recruit to the impact on your joints. Both workouts can boost your heart health, build endurance, and leave you seriously sweaty, but they place different demands on your body, according to Gab Reznik, CPT and Tone House coach. The question isn’t which is better across the board—it’s which is better for you depending on your goals.

Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.

At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.

In a recent development, “Any movement is better than no movement at all—whether that’s incline walking or running,” Reznik tells SELF. “They’re both effective at increasing blood flow, elevating heart rate, and improving overall aerobic capacity.” That means stronger heart and lung function over time—which are key markers of long-term health.

In a recent development, they also both demand muscular effort. Running requires you to generate power with every stride, while incline walking emphasizes controlled, deliberate steps against gravity (thanks to the incline). “Over time, the repetitive impact and loading can help strengthen joints and support long-term durability when done properly,” Reznik claims.

While they may look similar on the surface, incline walking and running are different in two major ways: how hard they push your body, and how much stress they place on your joints.

In a recent development, running is the higher-impact option. With each stride, your joints absorb roughly two to three times your body weight. That added force typically translates to higher intensity—and more calories burned per hour, Reznik explains.

In a recent development, incline walking, on the other hand, keeps one foot on the ground at all times, reducing overall joint load. “Incline walking is more sustainable for longer durations,” Reznik states. “At the same fitness level, someone will typically be able to maintain an incline walk longer than a run due to the lower per-step demand.”.

It’s easy to think of incline walking as purely cardio—but that’s only part of its benefits.

According to recent reports, “Incline walking can absolutely build strength, just not in the same way as lifting weights,” Reznik says. Instead of maximizing muscle growth by picking up heavy weights, incline walking improves muscular endurance, particularly in the lower body (think: glutes, hamstrings, and calves).

Sources indicate that the steeper the incline, the greater the challenge. And if you want to level up even more, try adding external load, like a weighted vest, Reznik suggests. “It can increase the strength stimulus without significantly increasing joint impact.”.

Still, it’s important to keep your expectations realistic. If your goal is to build maximal strength or increase muscle size, traditional strength training should still be your primary focus.

One of the biggest misconceptions about incline walking is that it’s somehow inferior to running. Reznik is quick to shut that down.

“Walking isn’t less effective—it’s simply a different type of stimulus,” she states.

According to recent reports, in fact, incline walking can be deceptively tough. Imagine this: a 15% incline at 3 mph for 30 minutes, without holding onto the treadmill. “That’s extremely challenging—even for a trained runner,” Reznik indicates.

Both workouts can improve cardiovascular fitness and support fat loss when programmed appropriately. The key is understanding that “effective” doesn’t mean “hardest”—it means the movement is aligned with your fitness goals.

If you’re aiming to maximize calorie burn in a shorter amount of time or really test your cardiovascular endurance, running may be the more efficient choice, Reznik says. Its higher intensity makes it ideal for pushing your limits.

According to recent reports, but if you’re looking to reduce joint stress while still building aerobic fitness (and even some muscular endurance), incline walking may be the smarter pick. “If you treat them as complementary, you can unlock a higher level of performance and longevity,” Reznik states.

Deciding between incline walking and running ultimately comes down to three factors: your goals, your current fitness level, and what you actually enjoy enough to stick with.

Beginners might start with a light jog at a conversational pace or a slight incline (around 2% to 3%) at a comfortable walking speed, Reznik suggests. From there, it’s vital to progress either the speed or incline, but not both at once.

Recent findings suggest that “Incline walking isn’t the ‘easy’ option—it’s the smart option when used correctly,” Reznik indicates. “Running isn’t the ‘better’ option—it’s the specific option when it aligns with your goals.”.

A well-rounded routine might include both: running for higher-intensity days when you want to challenge your cardio limits, and incline walking for longer, lower-impact sessions that still deliver a serious burn.

Ultimately, there’s no clear winner between incline walking and running because they aren’t rivals. Both movements can be tools for improving heart health, building endurance and strengthening key muscle groups. The better workout is the one that helps you move consistently and safely. And in many cases, the smartest approach isn’t choosing between them—it’s using both.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there's a moment in GTA 6 where Lucia is carrying drinks, her hands are full, and she turns around and bumps a door open with her hip. It's an animation repeated throughout the game, subtle but realistic. I picked up on this in my GTA 6 review when Lucia buys a shake and ice cream and has to nudge the door with her hip to get through.

It’s tiny and incidental. It’s also, according to Rockstar’s animators, the kind of thing that took months to get right. I can see why this, along with other little animation flourishes, such as the way Lucia and Jason pull bag straps over their heads to shoulder a loot sack or how they climb in and out of cars, windows, and straddle bikes – little animation touches that build realism.

Industry observers note that mike Jones, Director of Animation: Gameplay Animation, notes the aim from the start was a game that felt “fast and responsive yet maintain a weight which grounds our world in realism”. Red Dead Redemption 2 had a slower heartbeat that suited its setting, he says. “Jason and Lucia’s world demands a faster pacing to interactions and movement.”.

That pace comes with detail attached. “We put a huge effort into the details,” Jones says, “which means teams caring about something as mundane as how the players might use a door when carrying drinks.”.

In a recent development, the result is Lucia turning her back to push through with her hip while her hands are occupied. “That took months of development,” Jones states, “but it matters.”.

Moving around is a big part of that. Jones indicates traversal is “far more fluid than anything we’ve achieved before”, with vaulting and climbing designed to keep your momentum. There are “countless variations” depending on how you trigger an action, and you can branch out and chain jumps together, with the landing changing too.

Rooftops are where it really pays off. “The amount of visual detail on the roofs of buildings is astounding,” Jones indicates, “and the traversal allows for some breathtaking foot chases.”.

It's true, I've spent hours in GTA 6 parkouring around warehouse rooftops looking for entrances and secrets. The animation flows with realism, and Lucia and Jason handle ledges and windows differently. Just brilliant.

Mark Tennant, Vice President of Animation, says the physical side of the partnership needed “a lot of thought and iteration”. Players can interact with their partner in “a natural, loving way”, with “a believable progression based on their overall investment in the relationship”.

The animators had to find “a realistic balance between player agency and partner response while keeping things fun, passionate, and rewarding”, Tennant indicates.

Sources indicate that all of that sits on top of the everyday stuff. Tennant states there are “close to a thousand animation sets for ambient activities”, plus “hundreds of bespoke one-off events and custom sequences”. Keeping them consistent meant working closely with the design team across the whole world.

Industry observers note that you’ll never consciously notice most of it. But when a character can’t open a door without bumping a hip, it’s a sign Rockstar wants you to feel the weight of Leonida.

Photography by Syam Sreeshylam.

Curving ceilings sweep down to frame the two small gardens that flank this home in Kerala, India, designed by local architecture studio Fictional Project.

Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.

This led Fictional Project to pull the home’s built volume back to create space for two planted yards on either side, overlooked by the home’s pared-back and open interiors.

“The residence is careful not to overpower, becoming one with the landscape,” the studio told Dezeen.

Interstitial Living is organised around a bedroom at its centre, which is housed within a cubic volume finished in cement plaster.

A small window in this bedroom overlooks a potted tree within a cut-out in the floor of the adjacent living room, which faces the yard to the west through a row of full-height windows above a built-in timber bench.

On the opposite side of the home, the kitchen overlooks the eastern yard through a row of windows above its countertops. Both these spaces are defined by the curving white-plastered ceilings overhead, which sweep down from the centre of the home.

Industry observers note that “The scale of the residence allows for intimate working spaces in the kitchen and a welcoming living room, all accentuated by the dynamic nature of the roof. The other spaces negotiate the private/public nature of the indoors,” the studio explained.

“The concavity of the roof creates a visual connection to the outdoors, becoming a marker that emerges from within the site.”.

Recent findings suggest that “It breaks the rigidity of a traditional sloping roof, helping create fluid indoor spaces. Nothing here is built or conceived in isolation, but rather as interconnected systems,” it added.

The smaller first floor contains a second bedroom, bathroom and a study area, which overlook the living space below from a steel-framed landing and internal windows.

While the internal finishes were kept minimal, the exterior of the home and its boundary walls were built using terracotta-toned textured blocks, which the studio described as introducing a sense of “groundedness and warmth”.

Other dwellings in Kerala recently featured on Dezeen include a home by InLe Architects framed and shaded by two large mango trees and a farmhouse by Evolving Radical Aesthetics that is built into a hillside above a carved-out, open-air temple.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the years, the definition of the 'creative' has been in flux. No longer comprised of classically trained industry veterans, design has been democratised (for better or for worse, depending on who you ask), and Adobe continues to pioneer this adapting creative sphere.

According to recent reports, but what does the creative professional of 2026 look like? And with advancements like Adobe Firefly and the increasing development of AI tools, how does Adobe serve this ever-evolving industry without losing sight of the creatives that supported it from the start?

Sources indicate that to understand more, I sat down with Adobe's Vice President, Product Marketing for Creative Professionals, Deepa Subramaniam. Together, we discussed how the brand has grown with its creative consumers, and how Adobe is innovating for the next generation.

According to recent reports, ultimately, a creative professional is someone whose job it is to be creative – that can be as broad or as narrow a definition as you want. The job of a creative professional has dramatically changed: print to digital, digital to web, web to mobile, and now we are in this moment of things changing with AI. Workflows are changing; the expectations around creative work are changing because of what AI unlocks.

How they express that taste and how they put their creative expression out into the world is changing. They have more options for how they want to create: tools, agentic features, workflows in an app, mixing of modalities and categories. But still, the creative professional is the person with taste, creative vision and creative expression.

In a recent development, it's not our job to tell you how to create – it's our job to support you in how you want to create. It comes down to giving you choice. The anxieties get flared when you feel that there is no choice for you, like you're being led down a particular path rather than choosing that path intentionally for yourself.

Sources indicate that do you want to create in flagship applications that are hyper-specific and fantastic for a particular category of work? Photoshop for imaging, Premiere for video and audio editing, etc., or do you want to create in a more multimodal product like Firefly? Do you want to create with an agent in the sidecar or in the driver's seat?

Sources indicate that we're just trying to give you a lot of choice. I find that when you give creatives a choice, they make an informed decision. The anxiety lessens because it's the creative taking the steering wheel and making that choice. We want to give them a menu of options to see what kind of shots they can call.

Acknowledging that it's happening is the first step; then it's about helping to alleviate the pressure from the insatiable need for content. The need to create across different media formats, for different audiences, on different device types – it's challenging to stay on top of that.

But staying on top of that is crucial and necessary to keep navigating the industry. Acknowledging that is powerful – people look to Adobe to acknowledge and guide the way sometimes. AI does give a few ways for you to stay on top of that pressure for content, but not replace your creativity. It can augment your productivity so you can stay on top of all that growing expectation.

I wish I had a crystal ball. We're seeing an increasing need to touch every part of the creative lifecycle. You're ideating, you're creating, you're doing the post-production, you're scaling – that's only going to continue.

There is a move to creative professionals having a speciality, but also embracing being a generalist too. Like graphic designers being social media whizzes or video editors also being able to do sound and colour. There's still a need to be a specialist, but augmented with generalist capabilities in other mediums and categories. That's why we continue to focus on making our applications interconnected and multimodal because that pressure isn't going to go away.

In my mind, when I hear "creative professional," that's distinct from content creator or influencer – but maybe they're two sides of the same coin.

It's about creative vision. The role of a creative professional is changing rapidly from repetitive atomic tasks, allowing them to focus on higher-level creative thinking. Some see that as a blessing and a boon. Others see that as a pretty disruptive change to how they operate. Everyone's on their own journey of acknowledging and accepting that change. A creative professional's vision and direction are becoming much more important.

Sources indicate that oh yeah, definitely. I've talked to people who were staunchly like, "I have my creative process. Why should I change it? It's been my process for two decades." I absolutely meet people who are staunchly not interested in folding AI into their workflow. And when I've talked to them sometime down the road, often they have adopted some form of AI into their craft. Maybe it's subtle, maybe it's pointed, but I think that just speaks to the fact that everyone's on their own personal journey of evolving how they create.

At the same time, this next generation of creatives is entering the industry only knowing AI. There are creatives who learned and honed their craft well before AI models became a thing, and there are creatives right now who are learning their creative expression in real time alongside it. It's wild.

According to recent reports, because it can, when wielded appropriately, be a time saver. It's not meant to replace your creativity. It's meant to enhance your creativity. So you can be creative and get stuff done faster, and be more creative. I really believe that is where AI is valuable.

Whether it's creative craft or software development, AI can take the un-fun parts of your job off your plate to prioritise the fun parts of your job. That's the journey we've been on with integrating AI thoughtfully into our portfolio, and people's usage and reception of it seems to prove that we're onto something.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:.

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina states it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she notes it just represents overall traits.

Recent findings suggest that verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she states.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

Your sun sign is crucial, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Aman Group.

Fresh York studio SHoP Architects has released designs for a ribbed supertall skyscraper in Miami, announced alongside the launch of a luxury brand for which Serbian tennis player Novak Djokovic is developing amenity facilities.

SHoP Architects, who are behind some of Upcoming York City’s tallest buildings, designed the 1,049-foot-tall (320-metre-tall) skyscraper around ATMA, a luxury brand being rolled out by hospitality operator Aman Group.

If completed at the stated height, it would be taller than the city’s current tallest skyscraper, and have the same projected height as the in-progress Waldorf Astoria Hotel & Residences Miami, which has been cited as the city’s future tallest.

The skyscraper will include a hotel, residences and a members’ club. According to Aman Group, ATMA’s “advanced wellness programming and world-class sport facilities” will be developed “exclusively” with Djokovic, who is credited as a global partner of the new brand.

Designs for the skyscraper itself show a ribbed form of balconied terraces organised around a central void that runs from the crown to the podium.

It is planned for Miami’s Brickell neighbourhood, and Aman Group said that the floor-to-ceiling windows of the skyscraper will merge the “futuristic architecture with the bay”.

It has been revealed that toronto-based interiors outfit Studio Paolo Ferrari has been chosen as the interiors lead on the project. It will include condos with one to five bedrooms, with six-bedroom penthouses pushed to the top of the skyscraper.

The structure will have setbacks at the upper floors, presumably to create more panoramic views for residences in the penthouses.

The ATMA concept is based around what Aman Group calls “performance-driven lifestyle”.

“Monolithic architecture meets biomorphic design, furniture is shaped naturally to the human form and ambience adjusts sensitively to residents’ and guests’ circadian rhythm,” noted Aman Group.

Djokovic’s programme, meanwhile, will include a 120,000-square-foot spa and wellness centre.

“ATMA Miami will sit at the pinnacle of what performance living can achieve,” said Djokovic.

OKO Group and Oak Row Equities were declared as developers for the project.

In a recent development, SHoP Architects is no stranger to supertall luxury residences. It designed New York’s skinniest supertall skyscraper to have single-floor apartments on the city’s so-called Billionaires Row. It also designed the Brooklyn Tower, the tallest structure in the borough.

Images courtesy of Aman Group.

Latest Update: A New Study Reveals 3 Migraine Triggers That Might Be Making Your Headaches Worse—See Them Here

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week.
  • That’s the major takeaway from latest research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.
  • If you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week. But while you’re probably focused on staying cool, there’s one more thing that should be on your radar: a higher-than-usual risk of migraine headaches.

That’s the major takeaway from latest research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.

If you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket. Here’s what the study found, plus how doctors who treat patients with migraine recommend protecting yourself.

Industry observers note that for the study, researchers followed 7,032 people living in Israel for about a decade who suffered from migraines. During the study period, researchers looked at participants’ daily exposure to air pollution, along with tracking weather conditions. They also looked at how often and when people visited the hospital or their primary care doctor with a migraine. That data was compared to the levels of pollution and weather conditions on that particular day, along with seven days before that.

During the study period, 2,215 people (or 32%) had at least one visit to the hospital or a clinic with a migraine. The researchers also found that 47% of participants in the study bought triptan medications at one point or another—fast-acting prescription medications that are designed to stop a migraine—with most using at least two tablets a month.

Ultimately, the researchers discovered a link between three weather-related factors and migraine: air pollution, temperature (including UV exposure), and humidity. First, they found a correlation between higher levels of air pollution and the most number of visits to a hospital or clinic for a migraine. They also found that the day with the least visits to the hospital or clinic also had lower-than-average pollution levels. People with short-term exposure to high levels of nitrogen dioxide (a common pollutant from traffic exhaust) were 41% more likely to go to the hospital or clinic for migraine than people who weren’t exposed to high levels of the gas.

According to recent reports, the study also revealed that people who were exposed to high levels of UV rays from the sun on a given day were 23% more likely to visit a healthcare provider for migraine symptoms than those who weren’t. High temperatures and low humidity appear to be linked to more migraine headaches, likely because they amplify the effect of nitrogen dioxide, the researchers stated.

With climate change intensifying how often we deal with heat waves and pollution, it’s notable to consider these risk factors when it comes to migraine, the researchers wrote.

It’s important to note that the study didn’t prove that air pollution, heat, and lower humidity levels cause migraines—it just found a link between them. But doctors say there’s likely something here.

Air pollution can spark neuroinflammation (the immune system’s inflammatory response in the brain and spinal cord), which is a risk factor for migraine, Sana Ghafoor, MD, neurologist at Tufts Medical Center, tells SELF. This may cause a release of pain chemicals like calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P that can lead to a migraine, Dr. Ghafoor says.

Sources indicate that air pollution may be particularly problematic for people with allergies who also struggle with migraines, Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California, tells SELF. The body may see air pollution as an allergen and mount an immune response, which can spark a migraine in people who are sensitive to this trigger, he explains.

Then, there’s the fact that heat can impact blood vessels and nerves. “When people heat up, nerves and blood vessels in tight locations can become irritated, as the diameter of a blood vessel or nerves increases with heat,” Dr. Segil says. That, too, can trigger a migraine. You’re also more susceptible to getting dehydrated when it’s hot out, Dr. Ghafoor says: “If you're overheated and dehydrated, those can also trigger migraines.”.

Dr. Segil points out that high humidity common in the spring and summer (and not just that related to air pollution) can trigger migraines too. High humidity causes you to sweat and lose water, which can decrease the amount of blood in your blood vessels (if you don’t replace it), Dr. Segil claims. “This decreases the diameter of blood vessels and can cause headaches, just like an increased blood vessel diameter,” he says.

Dr. Ghafoor says she often sees more patients have migraine headaches when high humidity strikes. “Even with small [atmospheric] pressure changes, it can activate nerve endings and sinuses, which can lead to the release of pain chemicals,” she says.

These are some of the most common migraine triggers, according to the US National Library of Medicine:.

These foods and ingredients can also trigger migraines, per the US National Library of Medicine:.

Migraine triggers are personal, making it important to do what you can to figure out yours and then try to avoid them as best as possible. (Dr. Ghafoor recommends keeping a headache diary to try to narrow things down.) But factors like air pollution, heat, and humidity can be tough to avoid.

In a recent development, if levels of air pollution are high in your area, Dr. Segil recommends wearing a face mask like an N95 when you need to be outdoors. Keeping your windows shut and running an air purifier can also help tamp down on pollution indoors. If you’d like, you can track pollution levels throughout the day and try to stay inside during peak times, Dr. Ghafoor says.

It has been revealed that when heat and humidity strikes, Dr. Ghafoor recommends doing what you can to stay well hydrated. “Make sure that it’s not just water, but electrolytes too,” she claims. “All of that is a very key part of lifestyle management for patients who have migraine.”.

Sources indicate that ultimately, doing your best to try to figure out your triggers (and avoid them) can go a long way toward helping to keep you more comfortable on a regular basis. “Knowing and identifying migraine triggers is very important,” Dr. Ghafoor says. “It’s empowering the patient to understand their disease.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

For wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

Sources indicate that for starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

It’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research demonstrates that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study indicated that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

In a recent development, on the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

In a recent development, by training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

As a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

Then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

Sources indicate that wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

In a recent development, it all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

Meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Sources indicate that yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

According to recent reports, or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

Recent findings suggest that no matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”.

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by James Brittain (unless stated otherwise).

Canadian studio Sid Lee Architecture has created a curved-glass hotel that takes cues from the burgeoning wine region of Ontario.

The Montreal-based studio recently unveiled The Clayfield Hotel, a 60-room hotel with a restaurant, ballroom and rooftop terrace in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

The rounded 94,000-square-foot (8,732-square metre) hotel sits on a property in the historic village that is being transformed by winemakers.

“The Clayfield was conceived as a new hub for Niagara-on-the-Lake, a place where wine culture and hospitality find a home,” Martin Leblanc, architect and co-founding partner of Sid Lee Architecture, told Dezeen.

“Its layered contours, rounded geometry and rhythmic wood elements translate the surrounding vineyard landscape into a building that celebrates the region’s contribution to Canadian winemaking.”.

The hotel was conceived as a pavilion set in the emerging townscape between vineyards and the Clayfield Commons housing development on an agricultural road.

The curved form allows access and connection to its surroundings in multiple directions.

“The hotel acts as a threshold between these typologies, connecting the vineyard and the denser village-like development around it,” Leblanc stated.

“Its exterior wood elements recall the rhythm of the vine rows, the layered concrete refers to the clay soil and the reflective glass registers the changing light, sky and seasons.”.

The studio said that the organic, natural flow of a hotel is essential to the lasting success of the design.

Working back and forth between the architecture and the interior design, the studio laid out spaces to progress from public to private and back again, integrating moments for visitors to discover the landscape.

Recent findings suggest that “As visitors approach and circulate around the building, it frames changing views of the vines, the plaza and the emerging neighbourhood,” Leblanc remarked. “The lobby acts as a gateway to the vineyard, while the rooftop terrace reconnects the hotel experience with its broader surroundings.”.

Meanwhile, the staircase acts as a connector, transition and centrepiece between the plaza, lobby and upper levels.

“Inside, we chose a palette that speaks to the natural beauty of Niagara’s wine country: walnut panelling, concrete, dark amaranth-coloured leather, greige limestone and woven fabrics,” Leblanc said, calling out the limestone registration desk chiselled from the Niagara Escarpment and the restaurant’s curved bar that resembles the shape of the building.

With mostly Teknion furniture, each space represents a season of the vineyard, from spring in the lobby to winter in the guest rooms with more quiet, reserved furnishings that complete the rooms that fan out from the rounded concrete strata.

Sources indicate that founded in 2009, Sid Lee Architecture has six offices across North America and Europe. The studio previously remodelled its own offices in an I.M. Pei office building, overhauled the interiors of the iconic Fairmont Queen Elizabeth Hotel and created an artisan-inspired workplace for video game designers – all in Montreal.

#125765. GTA 6 is proof that human creativity is still the most impressive technology we have

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (957 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Creativebloq ↗ Open Full Page

GTA 6 is proof that human creativity is still the most impressive technology we have

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that every week, another AI tool promises to conjure images, environments and characters from a few lines of text.
  • I've spent weeks exploring Rockstar's Leonida, and while GTA 6 is graphically stunning, it's the little things I keep coming back to.
  • Rockstar has said it designs buildings by imagining who would live in them and how they'd spend their days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that every week, another AI tool promises to conjure images, environments and characters from a few lines of text. Autodesk and Adobe are among those promising to make creating worlds and bringing ideas to life easier, often with little more than a prompt. Then I spent three weeks playing GTA 6, and it reminded me why I still find artists and designers so bloody impressive.

I've spent weeks exploring Rockstar's Leonida, and while GTA 6 is graphically stunning, it's the little things I keep coming back to. The shopfront branding, flyers that lead you to new characters, comic books on shelves, graffiti and fake adverts. Even Vice City's layout has a personality: all spaghetti junctions, back alleys and beachfront hotels, a world away from the calmer, goofier northern islands.

Rockstar has said it designs buildings by imagining who would live in them and how they'd spend their days. "For every visual design, we are getting into the heads of the people who would have inhabited that place and role-playing how the final look would have come about," says Miriam Bellard, Vice President of Art: Visual Development, in my interview with the studio. I love that approach. You aren't just making a building look convincing; you're thinking about the person who might have put that sofa there, chosen that colour or let the garden get overgrown.

The same thought goes into the animation, to the extent that Rockstar spent months perfecting how Lucia opens a door with her hip. I properly laughed out loud when a very large resident giggled, stumbled and tipped over a railing into a river. In one bar, a drunk woman trails Jason around, being annoying in exactly the way drunk people are. There's a sequence where you drunkenly try to find your hotel room, and it's the kind of disorientation many of us have felt, both with alcohol and with modern architecture where every corridor looks the same. Out in the woods, two deer nuzzle each other. These little moments don't advance the plot, but they're the sort of thing that makes me want to keep exploring.

Sources indicate that the weather is another thing I've found myself stopping to look at, from morning sun cutting through mist over wildflower meadows to storm clouds swallowing the skyline. Rain changes what you can see and hear, and flying a plane through a storm is shaky, stubborn and hard. In a nightclub, smoke and reflected light leave you disoriented, just as they should. In fact, Rockstar has spent years hiding GTA 6's environmental storytelling in details you might never notice. There's an awful lot of work behind getting these moments right, and you can feel it when you're playing.

Recent findings suggest that I've also been surprised by how much I care about Jason and Lucia, and how much of that comes down to the game's art, design and animation. I caught myself shooting enemies in the arms and legs instead of finishing them off because I wanted Lucia to think well of Jason, and because it gets too grim to kill people in a game that looks this realistic. It's an odd thing to admit about GTA, but I started feeling uncomfortable with some of the violence. The writing, animation, and character design had me invested in two people who don't exist in a world built in polygons.

There's a lot of noise about AI generating images, making environments and producing assets faster, and I can see the appeal, but creativity goes well beyond making something that looks good. It's the decisions about what goes into a scene, what gets left out, how a character reacts, when a joke lands and how some seemingly insignificant detail can make someone feel something. You don't necessarily notice any of this when it's done well, which is probably why it's so easy to overlook.

Sources indicate that I'm not anti-technology, and artists have always grabbed upcoming tools. I'm sure AI will find its place, especially in taking the drudgery out of production, but there's a difference between helping an artist work and replacing the decisions that make their work interesting. The latest GDC industry research is interesting reading: 55% of surveyed game industry professionals believe generative AI is having a negative impact on the games industry, while 40% say they use it in their jobs. There's clearly an appetite for practical applications, but that doesn't mean people want AI making their creative decisions.

Recent findings suggest that leonida is full of thousands of small human choices, from subtle animated gestures to authentically made magazines, fictional advertising and modern art sculptures. I've spent weeks wandering around this place, and I'm still finding things to look at. That's a remarkable achievement, and one that makes me appreciate the people behind it all the more. After all the talk of AI being able to generate anything, I still think the most impressive thing is what happens when thousands of people put their imagination, experience and judgement into making something together.

Industry observers note that ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian rolled out Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal.
  • In a recent development, at the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy.
  • If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal. It was sharp, persistent, and unsettling in a way I couldn’t ignore. As a former labor and delivery nurse, I understood the risks in a way many patients do not. I knew what to watch for. I knew my history. I knew when something felt wrong. Yet when I raised concerns, they were not met with the urgency they deserved.

In a recent development, at the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy. I knew that the vertical incision on my uterus could put a future pregnancy at risk. I spoke up. I asked questions. I paid attention to my body. Still, when I experienced a uterine rupture, I was navigating a system that did not respond with the level of care and urgency that the moment required.

If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?

Conversations during Black Maternal Health Week often center around one urgent truth: Black women are still far more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes in this country than white women. This is not an assumption. It is a proven fact, and it should stop all of us in our tracks. It also does not only impact one socioeconomic group. It affects everyone, including some of the most visible and resourced women in the world.

Recent findings suggest that as the founder of Mielle, my mission is to empower women, especially Black women, to express their authentic selves. At its core, that mission is about care, agency, and visibility, which is why conversations like this matter. It’s about showing up for every part of Black women’s experience. We need to talk more candidly about what happens to Black women who survive the trauma of miscarriage or stillbirth, and the prolonged mental health challenges that can follow, including postpartum depression.

Black women are expected to remain “strong” while navigating medical emergencies. We’re dismissed, told to wait, to calm down, and to trust a system that has not always earned that trust. We survive experiences that change our families and us forever. And then, too often, we are expected to do something just as impossible: keep going as if survival is the end of the story. It is not.

That is why Black Maternal Health Week cannot be about mortality alone. It must also be about what it means to live after trauma, preventable harm, and loss that reshapes your life.

The data make clear that this crisis is ongoing. Black women are about three times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes than white women, and more than 80% of those deaths are considered preventable. Black infants also die at more than twice the rate of white infants. These are not random gaps. They reflect a healthcare system and a culture that too often normalizes Black women’s pain instead of responding to it.

Research reveals that one in five women, or about 20%, report mistreatment during maternity care, but for Black women, that figure climbs to nearly 30%, reflecting more frequent experiences of bias, disrespect, and lack of autonomy in clinical settings. Nearly half of women say they have held back from asking questions or sharing concerns. In one of the most vulnerable moments of a person’s life, too many are already calculating whether speaking up will make things worse.

In a recent development, in my own life, grief did not arrive quietly. It entered my marriage, my motherhood, my body, my faith, and eventually my work. In my book, The Glory In Your Story, I write about how grief does not follow a timeline. It becomes part of who you are, and healing begins not by outrunning it, but by acknowledging it.

That matters because so many Black women are praised for being strong when what we actually need is space to be human. After losing Milan, I returned to work. I kept moving. I built Mielle. From the outside, it can look like a story of resilience. And in many ways, it is. But we have to be honest about the lessons we take from stories like mine.

Industry observers note that the lesson should not be that Black women are uniquely equipped to carry devastating grief and still perform at a high level. It should not be that our resilience makes systemic failures acceptable. And it should not be that we have to turn survival into something productive just to make our pain legible.

Too often, we celebrate the comeback without sitting long enough with the conditions that made it necessary.

It has been revealed that faith carried me. Purpose helped me rebuild. But none of that changes the reality that more listening, better care, stronger hospital systems, and greater urgency might have changed my story. If we are serious about maternal health, we have to be just as serious about saying that clearly.

Black Maternal Health Week gives us an opportunity to think more broadly about what justice looks like. It looks like hospitals are equipped for emergencies. It looks like providers who listen to Black women the first time, without requiring patients to fight to be believed. It looks like support for families after loss–not just during a crisis. And it looks like making space for grief without expecting Black women to turn it into inspiration before we are ready.

Recent findings suggest that it’s time that we honor not only the women we have lost, but also the women still here carrying what the system could not or would not hold for them. Survival is not the finish line. Being heard, protected, and cared for should be.

Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

📅 31 Aug 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cutting back on calories but not losing weight?
  • Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight.
  • The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”.

Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

Industry observers note that research highlights starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

Industry observers note that evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

What does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:.

Starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

Sources indicate that however, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

According to recent reports, most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

Industry observers note that so what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

Industry observers note that first, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Sources indicate that choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

Weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

In a recent development, that mentioned, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

Sources indicate that despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

Breaking: Cosentino supports architectural creativity with Ēclos mineral surface

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.
  • Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.
  • The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.

Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.

The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.

This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.

According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

According to recent reports, “For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” remarked the company. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”.

“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”.

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino says that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

“With Ēclos, the patterning is constructed within the slab rather than confined to its face,” continued the brand. “That makes the relationship between surface and depth an crucial part of the design conversation, particularly where edges remain visible.”.

“The interest lies not just in the appearance of the material, but in how it can be cut, assembled and brought into a project with adjacent finishes.”.

Its fabricators can advise how cutting, profiling, jointing and installation can help a designer’s vision come together.

The process can involve reviewing samples, fabrication drawings and, where appropriate, physical mock-ups.

“The position of a seam or the treatment of an exposed edge can subtly alter the proportions and perceived weight of an element,” remarked Cosentino.

“The aim is not necessarily to make every joint disappear, but to make each one deliberate.”.

“Whether the intention is a continuous volume or a clearly expressed assembly, the junction deserves as much consideration as the surface itself,” the brand continued.

Ēclos introduced earlier this year and joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surface worktops from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.

It is suitable for both residential and commercial environments and can be used on worktops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces.

The first Ēclos collection – Eclectic Veins – incorporates 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, all made with a minimum of 50 per cent recycled content.

The material is practical for everyday use, withstanding scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain.

It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 degrees Celsius, including contact with hot cookware.

To learn more about Cosentino and Ēclos, visit the company’s website.

#125760. Tech Report: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1695 w)
